Traditional Norwegian stringed instrument

Hardanger fiddle (hardingfele)[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/FeleHel_%282%29.jpg/250px-FeleHel_%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FeleHel_(2).jpg)

Video 1[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hardanger_Fiddle_-_St_Cecilia's_Hall.webm "Play video")[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hardanger_Fiddle_-_St_Cecilia's_Hall.webm)

Playing a hardanger fiddle

A **hardanger fiddle** ([Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _**hardingfele**_) is a traditional [stringed instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stringed_instrument "Stringed instrument") considered the national instrument of Norway. In modern designs, this type of [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") is very similar to the [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin "Violin"), though with eight or nine [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strings_(music) "Strings (music)") (rather than four as on a standard violin) and thinner [wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood "Wood"). The earliest known example of the _hardingfele_ is from 1651, made by Ole Jonsen Jaastad in [Hardanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger "Hardanger"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-1) Originally, the instrument had a rounder, narrower body.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-2) Around the year 1850, the modern layout with a body much like the violin became the norm.

The [F-holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-holes "F-holes") of the hardanger fiddle are distinctive, oftentimes with a more "sunken" appearance, and generally straighter edges (unlike the frilly, swirly F-holes of a violin). Four of the strings are strung and played like a violin, while the rest, named understrings or [sympathetic strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_strings "Sympathetic strings"), [resonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonate "Resonate") under the influence of the other four. These additional strings are tuned and secured with extra pegs at the top of the scroll, effectively doubling the length of a Hardingfele scroll when compared to a violin. The sympathetic strings, once fastened to their pegs, are funneled through a "hollow" constructed fingerboard, which is built differently than a violin's, being slightly higher and thicker to allow for these extra strings. The resonant strings lie on the center of the special bridge, attached to extra hooks (or fine-tuners) on the tailpiece. Carved out within the center of the bridge is a smaller secondary "bridge", or opening, designed specifically for these resonant strings to pass through. This is where the resonance is picked up and reverberated. As notes are played, the vibrations are sent through the bridge, where the sympathetics echo those notes.

The _hardingfele'_ s bridge is unique compared to other bowed instruments. It is somewhat taller and wider, resulting in the strings being slightly lower and further apart; this allows for the easy execution of double-stops (playing of two strings at once). A similar technique is seen in some American old-time and bluegrass fiddlers, who intentionally move their bridge back a few millimetres closer to the tailpiece, for better double-stops. This technique lowers the action, but may not make double stops easier, as the radius of the top of the bridge needs to flatten more to make double stops easier.

The _hardingfele_ is used mainly in the southwest part of Norway, whereas the ordinary violin (called _flatfele_, 'flat fiddle', or _vanlig fele_, 'common fiddle') is found elsewhere. The _hardingfele_ is used for dancing, accompanied by rhythmic loud foot stomping. It was also traditional for the fiddler to lead the bridal procession to the entrance of the church, but not inside.

The instrument is often highly decorated, with a carved animal (usually a [dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon "Dragon") or the [Lion of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Norway "Coat of arms of Norway")) or a carved woman's head as part of the [scroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scroll_(music) "Scroll (music)") at the top of the [pegbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegbox "Pegbox"), extensive [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_pearl "Mother of pearl")[inlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inlay "Inlay") on the [tailpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailpiece "Tailpiece") and [fingerboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerboard "Fingerboard"), and black ink decorations called '[rosing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemaling "Rosemaling")' on the body of the instrument. Pieces of bone are sometimes used to decorate the pegs and the edges of the instrument.

## Tunings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Tunings")]

See also: [_Scordatura_ in folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scordatura#Scordatura_in_folk_music "Scordatura")

Unlike the violin, the _hardingfele_ is a [transposing instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposing_instrument "Transposing instrument"), meaning [sheet music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet_music "Sheet music") for the _hardingfele_ is written in a key other than the one where the instrument sounds when it plays that music. Specifically, the _hardingfele_ is a D instrument,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-3) meaning that the _hardingfele_'s written [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(musical_note) "C (musical note)") corresponds to [D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D_(musical_note) "D (musical note)") on a non-transposing instrument, such as the [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano"). The notes given below for tunings are therefore relative to the _hardingfele_'s written A, not to a [concert A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_pitch "Concert pitch").

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Midtdetalj.jpg/250px-Midtdetalj.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Midtdetalj.jpg)

The strings on a _hardingfele_

The understrings are tuned to vibrate according to the main tuning. For example, when the main strings are tuned A-D-A-E, the understrings are tuned B-D-E-F♯-A.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-4) The tuning largely depends on the region in which the instrument is being played, or the requirements of a particular tune.

In Norway, more than 20 different tunings are recorded.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-5) Most hardanger tunes are played in a common tuning (A-D-A-E). The hardanger fiddle can also be played in "low bass", the word "bass" referring to the lowest string, (G-D-A-E), the normal violin tuning. In certain regions, the "Gorrlaus" (F-D-A-E) tuning is sometimes used. Many well-known players (such as [Annbjørg Lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annbj%C3%B8rg_Lien "Annbjørg Lien")) frequently employ E-scale tunings; i.e., instead of A-D-A-E, with tunes being mainly played in a D-scale, the instrument will be tuned to B-E-B-F#, so the tunes are mostly in an E-scale. Going higher still, the player [Knut Buen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knut_Buen "Knut Buen") recorded several albums in an F-scale tuning, C-F-C-G. This is possible only on a smaller-bodied instrument (such as a hardanger fiddle), being rarely attempted on a standard full-sized violin. As a substitute, many fiddlers who play standard violins will simply tune their G string to A, using the A-D-A-E tuning, enabling them to play the same style of music.

Another tuning is called "[troll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troll "Troll") tuning" (A-E-A-C♯). Troll tuning is used for the [fanitullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanitullen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fanitullen (page does not exist)")[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/fanitullen "no:fanitullen")] tunes, also called the [devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil_in_Christianity "Devil in Christianity")'s tunes, as well as the tunes from the [Kivlemøyane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kivlem%C3%B8yane "Kivlemøyane") suite (thus associated with the [hulderpeople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulder "Hulder") as well as the devil). In the [Valdres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdres "Valdres")[district of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Norway "Districts of Norway"), using this particular tuning is called "greylighting", a reminder that the fiddler tuned his fiddle like this when the morning was near, and he had played himself through a number of other tunings.

Legend has it that the fiddler learned _fanitullen_ tunes from the devil. This tuning limits the melodic range of the tunes and is therefore sparsely used.

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Technique")]

The technique of bowing a _hardingfele_ also differs from that used with a violin. It's a smoother, bouncier style of bowing, with a lighter touch. The player usually bows on two of the upper strings at a time, and sometimes three. This is made easy by the relative flatness of the bridge, unlike the more curved bridge on a violin. The objective is to create a continuous sound of two (or more due to the sympathetic understrings) pitches. The strings of the fiddle are slimmer than those of the violin, resembling the strings of violins from the [baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") period. Many classically trained violinists use a baroque bow when playing the _hardingfele_ in order to counteract the extra weight that classical violinists naturally place on the string.

Here is an example of technique shown by Rose Logan with an instrument held at [St Cecilia's Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Cecilia's_Hall "St Cecilia's Hall").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-6)

## The hardanger fiddle and religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The hardanger fiddle and religion")]

The _hardingfele_ has had a long history with the Christian church. Well known early fiddle maker Isak Botnen is said to have learned some of his craft from church lay leader and school master Lars Klark, along with the methods for varnishing from pastor Dedrik Muus.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-7) In many folktales, the devil is associated with the _hardingfele_; in fact many good players were said to have been taught to play by the devil, if not by the [nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neck_(water_spirit) "Neck (water spirit)"). During religious revivals in the 19th century, many fiddles (regular and hardanger)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-8) were destroyed or hidden both by fiddlers and laypeople who thought "that it would be best for the soul that the fiddles be burned", as it was viewed as a "sinful instrument that encouraged wild dances, drinking and fights."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-9) This happened in Norway, as well as other parts of Europe, and until the 20th century playing a hardanger fiddle in a church building was forbidden.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-autogenerated1-10) Some fiddlers, however, played on, in spite of all condemnation, and thus valuable traditions remained intact. The first folk musicians to perform in a church were the fiddlers [Johannes Dahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Dahle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Johannes Dahle (page does not exist)")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-11) from [Tinn Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinn_Municipality "Tinn Municipality"), and [Gjermund Haugen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gjermund_Haugen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gjermund Haugen (page does not exist)")[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gjermund%20Haugen "no:Gjermund Haugen")] from [Notodden Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notodden_Municipality "Notodden Municipality"). Dahle performed in the 1920s.

Known modern fiddler [Annbjørg Lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annbj%C3%B8rg_Lien "Annbjørg Lien") has played with church organist Iver Kleive,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-12) but even she has experienced prejudice before performance from the religious side.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-13) Also, the oldest known fiddles still in existence can be heard accompanied by the oldest playable church pipe organ in Norway (originally built for an 18th-century church) on the album "Rosa i Botnen" by Knut Hamre and Benedicte Maurseth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-autogenerated1-10) While the use of a _hardingfele_ in church in Norway may still be a bit sensitive for some, fiddlers in other parts of the world have no problems playing in churches for all types of occasions, including weddings.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-15)

## Influences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Influences")]

[Edvard Grieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Grieg "Edvard Grieg") adapted many hardanger folk tunes into his compositions, and composed tunes for the hardanger as part of his score for [Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibsen "Ibsen")'s _[Peer Gynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer\_Gynt "Peer Gynt")_ Suite No. 1. The opening phrase of "[Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning_Mood "Morning Mood")" from Grieg's _Peer Gynt_ music is derived from the tuning of the sympathetic strings of the hardanger fiddle: A F♯ E D E F♯ and so on.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-16)

In recent years, the instrument has gained recognition in the rest of the world. Japan has been one of the countries that has found an interest in the hardingfele and Japanese musicians travel to Norway just to learn to play this instrument. In 1997, the Australian [classical composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music")[Liza Lim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liza_Lim "Liza Lim") wrote the piece _Philtre_ for a solo hardanger fiddle, and she also includes the instrument in her work _Winding Bodies: 3 Knots_ (2013–14).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-18) Her string quartet _The Weaver's Knot_ (2013–14) is inspired by the sound and performance techniques of hardanger fiddle playing. Another recent work is "mobius II" for hardanger fiddle and electronics by the British composer Rose Dodd (2011, premiered at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival by Britt Pernille Froholm).

## Use in film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Use in film")]

The hardanger fiddle was used in the [soundtracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundtrack "Soundtrack") of _[The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings:\_The\_Two\_Towers "The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers")_, and _[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings:\_The\_Return\_of\_the\_King "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King")_ composed by [Howard Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Shore "Howard Shore"), to provide the main voice for the [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohan_(Middle-earth) "Rohan (Middle-earth)") theme. The use of the hardanger fiddle in this movie, however, is far from traditional: the theme does not use the idiomatic double stops, and the violinist also used vibrato, which is not traditionally used. It was also used by composer John Powell and played by Dermot Crehan in the DreamWorks film _[How to Train Your Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How\_to\_Train\_Your\_Dragon\_(2010\_film) "How to Train Your Dragon (2010 film)")_ for the main romantic theme.

The hardanger fiddle is also featured in the soundtrack of _[Armageddon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armageddon\_(1998\_film) "Armageddon (1998 film)")_ (composed by [Trevor Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Rabin "Trevor Rabin")), and in _[Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo\_(1996\_film) "Fargo (1996 film)")_ (composed by [Carter Burwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Burwell "Carter Burwell")). In the latter, the context is a little more traditional—the main theme it plays is an arrangement of a Norwegian folk song entitled "The Lost Sheep".

[Steven Van Zandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Van_Zandt "Steven Van Zandt") used the hardanger fiddle in the theme song he wrote for the TV series _[Lilyhammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilyhammer "Lilyhammer")_.

In the Japanese animated movie _[Tales from Earthsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Earthsea\_(film) "Tales from Earthsea (film)")_ it is played by [Rio Yamase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Yamase "Rio Yamase").

The hardanger fiddle is featured in the soundtrack of the 2017 film _[Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk\_(2017\_film) "Dunkirk (2017 film)")_, as well as the soundtrack for the 2021 _[Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki\_(TV\_series) "Loki (TV series)")_ series.

Traditional Norwegian stringed instrument

Playing a hardanger fiddle

A **hardanger fiddle** ([Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _**hardingfele**_) is a traditional [stringed instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stringed_instrument "Stringed instrument") considered the national instrument of Norway. In modern designs, this type of [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") is very similar to the [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin "Violin"), though with eight or nine [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strings_(music) "Strings (music)") (rather than four as on a standard violin) and thinner [wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood "Wood"). The earliest known example of the _hardingfele_ is from 1651, made by Ole Jonsen Jaastad in [Hardanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger "Hardanger"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-1) Originally, the instrument had a rounder, narrower body.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-2) Around the year 1850, the modern layout with a body much like the violin became the norm.

The [F-holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-holes "F-holes") of the hardanger fiddle are distinctive, oftentimes with a more "sunken" appearance, and generally straighter edges (unlike the frilly, swirly F-holes of a violin). Four of the strings are strung and played like a violin, while the rest, named understrings or [sympathetic strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_strings "Sympathetic strings"), [resonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonate "Resonate") under the influence of the other four. These additional strings are tuned and secured with extra pegs at the top of the scroll, effectively doubling the length of a Hardingfele scroll when compared to a violin. The sympathetic strings, once fastened to their pegs, are funneled through a "hollow" constructed fingerboard, which is built differently than a violin's, being slightly higher and thicker to allow for these extra strings. The resonant strings lie on the center of the special bridge, attached to extra hooks (or fine-tuners) on the tailpiece. Carved out within the center of the bridge is a smaller secondary "bridge", or opening, designed specifically for these resonant strings to pass through. This is where the resonance is picked up and reverberated. As notes are played, the vibrations are sent through the bridge, where the sympathetics echo those notes.

The _hardingfele'_ s bridge is unique compared to other bowed instruments. It is somewhat taller and wider, resulting in the strings being slightly lower and further apart; this allows for the easy execution of double-stops (playing of two strings at once). A similar technique is seen in some American old-time and bluegrass fiddlers, who intentionally move their bridge back a few millimetres closer to the tailpiece, for better double-stops. This technique lowers the action, but may not make double stops easier, as the radius of the top of the bridge needs to flatten more to make double stops easier.

The _hardingfele_ is used mainly in the southwest part of Norway, whereas the ordinary violin (called _flatfele_, 'flat fiddle', or _vanlig fele_, 'common fiddle') is found elsewhere. The _hardingfele_ is used for dancing, accompanied by rhythmic loud foot stomping. It was also traditional for the fiddler to lead the bridal procession to the entrance of the church, but not inside.

The instrument is often highly decorated, with a carved animal (usually a [dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon "Dragon") or the [Lion of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Norway "Coat of arms of Norway")) or a carved woman's head as part of the [scroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scroll_(music) "Scroll (music)") at the top of the [pegbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegbox "Pegbox"), extensive [mother of pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_pearl "Mother of pearl")[inlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inlay "Inlay") on the [tailpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailpiece "Tailpiece") and [fingerboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerboard "Fingerboard"), and black ink decorations called '[rosing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemaling "Rosemaling")' on the body of the instrument. Pieces of bone are sometimes used to decorate the pegs and the edges of the instrument.

## Tunings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Tunings")]

See also: [_Scordatura_ in folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scordatura#Scordatura_in_folk_music "Scordatura")

Unlike the violin, the _hardingfele_ is a [transposing instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposing_instrument "Transposing instrument"), meaning [sheet music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet_music "Sheet music") for the _hardingfele_ is written in a key other than the one where the instrument sounds when it plays that music. Specifically, the _hardingfele_ is a D instrument,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-3) meaning that the _hardingfele_'s written [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(musical_note) "C (musical note)") corresponds to [D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D_(musical_note) "D (musical note)") on a non-transposing instrument, such as the [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano"). The notes given below for tunings are therefore relative to the _hardingfele_'s written A, not to a [concert A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_pitch "Concert pitch").

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Midtdetalj.jpg/250px-Midtdetalj.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Midtdetalj.jpg)

The strings on a _hardingfele_

The understrings are tuned to vibrate according to the main tuning. For example, when the main strings are tuned A-D-A-E, the understrings are tuned B-D-E-F♯-A.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-4) The tuning largely depends on the region in which the instrument is being played, or the requirements of a particular tune.

In Norway, more than 20 different tunings are recorded.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-5) Most hardanger tunes are played in a common tuning (A-D-A-E). The hardanger fiddle can also be played in "low bass", the word "bass" referring to the lowest string, (G-D-A-E), the normal violin tuning. In certain regions, the "Gorrlaus" (F-D-A-E) tuning is sometimes used. Many well-known players (such as [Annbjørg Lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annbj%C3%B8rg_Lien "Annbjørg Lien")) frequently employ E-scale tunings; i.e., instead of A-D-A-E, with tunes being mainly played in a D-scale, the instrument will be tuned to B-E-B-F#, so the tunes are mostly in an E-scale. Going higher still, the player [Knut Buen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knut_Buen "Knut Buen") recorded several albums in an F-scale tuning, C-F-C-G. This is possible only on a smaller-bodied instrument (such as a hardanger fiddle), being rarely attempted on a standard full-sized violin. As a substitute, many fiddlers who play standard violins will simply tune their G string to A, using the A-D-A-E tuning, enabling them to play the same style of music.

Another tuning is called "[troll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troll "Troll") tuning" (A-E-A-C♯). Troll tuning is used for the [fanitullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanitullen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fanitullen (page does not exist)")[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/fanitullen "no:fanitullen")] tunes, also called the [devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil_in_Christianity "Devil in Christianity")'s tunes, as well as the tunes from the [Kivlemøyane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kivlem%C3%B8yane "Kivlemøyane") suite (thus associated with the [hulderpeople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulder "Hulder") as well as the devil). In the [Valdres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdres "Valdres")[district of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Norway "Districts of Norway"), using this particular tuning is called "greylighting", a reminder that the fiddler tuned his fiddle like this when the morning was near, and he had played himself through a number of other tunings.

Legend has it that the fiddler learned _fanitullen_ tunes from the devil. This tuning limits the melodic range of the tunes and is therefore sparsely used.

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Technique")]

The technique of bowing a _hardingfele_ also differs from that used with a violin. It's a smoother, bouncier style of bowing, with a lighter touch. The player usually bows on two of the upper strings at a time, and sometimes three. This is made easy by the relative flatness of the bridge, unlike the more curved bridge on a violin. The objective is to create a continuous sound of two (or more due to the sympathetic understrings) pitches. The strings of the fiddle are slimmer than those of the violin, resembling the strings of violins from the [baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") period. Many classically trained violinists use a baroque bow when playing the _hardingfele_ in order to counteract the extra weight that classical violinists naturally place on the string.

Here is an example of technique shown by Rose Logan with an instrument held at [St Cecilia's Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Cecilia's_Hall "St Cecilia's Hall").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-6)

## The hardanger fiddle and religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The hardanger fiddle and religion")]

The _hardingfele_ has had a long history with the Christian church. Well known early fiddle maker Isak Botnen is said to have learned some of his craft from church lay leader and school master Lars Klark, along with the methods for varnishing from pastor Dedrik Muus.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-7) In many folktales, the devil is associated with the _hardingfele_; in fact many good players were said to have been taught to play by the devil, if not by the [nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neck_(water_spirit) "Neck (water spirit)"). During religious revivals in the 19th century, many fiddles (regular and hardanger)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-8) were destroyed or hidden both by fiddlers and laypeople who thought "that it would be best for the soul that the fiddles be burned", as it was viewed as a "sinful instrument that encouraged wild dances, drinking and fights."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-9) This happened in Norway, as well as other parts of Europe, and until the 20th century playing a hardanger fiddle in a church building was forbidden.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-autogenerated1-10) Some fiddlers, however, played on, in spite of all condemnation, and thus valuable traditions remained intact. The first folk musicians to perform in a church were the fiddlers [Johannes Dahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Dahle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Johannes Dahle (page does not exist)")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-11) from [Tinn Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinn_Municipality "Tinn Municipality"), and [Gjermund Haugen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gjermund_Haugen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gjermund Haugen (page does not exist)")[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gjermund%20Haugen "no:Gjermund Haugen")] from [Notodden Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notodden_Municipality "Notodden Municipality"). Dahle performed in the 1920s.

Known modern fiddler [Annbjørg Lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annbj%C3%B8rg_Lien "Annbjørg Lien") has played with church organist Iver Kleive,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-12) but even she has experienced prejudice before performance from the religious side.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-13) Also, the oldest known fiddles still in existence can be heard accompanied by the oldest playable church pipe organ in Norway (originally built for an 18th-century church) on the album "Rosa i Botnen" by Knut Hamre and Benedicte Maurseth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-autogenerated1-10) While the use of a _hardingfele_ in church in Norway may still be a bit sensitive for some, fiddlers in other parts of the world have no problems playing in churches for all types of occasions, including weddings.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-15)

## Influences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Influences")]

[Edvard Grieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Grieg "Edvard Grieg") adapted many hardanger folk tunes into his compositions, and composed tunes for the hardanger as part of his score for [Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibsen "Ibsen")'s _[Peer Gynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer\_Gynt "Peer Gynt")_ Suite No. 1. The opening phrase of "[Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning_Mood "Morning Mood")" from Grieg's _Peer Gynt_ music is derived from the tuning of the sympathetic strings of the hardanger fiddle: A F♯ E D E F♯ and so on.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-16)

In recent years, the instrument has gained recognition in the rest of the world. Japan has been one of the countries that has found an interest in the hardingfele and Japanese musicians travel to Norway just to learn to play this instrument. In 1997, the Australian [classical composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music")[Liza Lim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liza_Lim "Liza Lim") wrote the piece _Philtre_ for a solo hardanger fiddle, and she also includes the instrument in her work _Winding Bodies: 3 Knots_ (2013–14).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardanger_fiddle#cite_note-18) Her string quartet _The Weaver's Knot_ (2013–14) is inspired by the sound and performance techniques of hardanger fiddle playing. Another recent work is "mobius II" for hardanger fiddle and electronics by the British composer Rose Dodd (2011, premiered at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival by Britt Pernille Froholm).

## Use in film

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hardanger_fiddle&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Use in film")]

The hardanger fiddle was used in the [soundtracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundtrack "Soundtrack") of _[The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings:\_The\_Two\_Towers "The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers")_, and _[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lord\_of\_the\_Rings:\_The\_Return\_of\_the\_King "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King")_ composed by [Howard Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Shore "Howard Shore"), to provide the main voice for the [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohan_(Middle-earth) "Rohan (Middle-earth)") theme. The use of the hardanger fiddle in this movie, however, is far from traditional: the theme does not use the idiomatic double stops, and the violinist also used vibrato, which is not traditionally used. It was also used by composer John Powell and played by Dermot Crehan in the DreamWorks film _[How to Train Your Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How\_to\_Train\_Your\_Dragon\_(2010\_film) "How to Train Your Dragon (2010 film)")_ for the main romantic theme.

The hardanger fiddle is also featured in the soundtrack of _[Armageddon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armageddon\_(1998\_film) "Armageddon (1998 film)")_ (composed by [Trevor Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Rabin "Trevor Rabin")), and in _[Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo\_(1996\_film) "Fargo (1996 film)")_ (composed by [Carter Burwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Burwell "Carter Burwell")). In the latter, the context is a little more traditional—the main theme it plays is an arrangement of a Norwegian folk song entitled "The Lost Sheep".

[Steven Van Zandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Van_Zandt "Steven Van Zandt") used the hardanger fiddle in the theme song he wrote for the TV series _[Lilyhammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilyhammer "Lilyhammer")_.

In the Japanese animated movie _[Tales from Earthsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Earthsea\_(film) "Tales from Earthsea (film)")_ it is played by [Rio Yamase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Yamase "Rio Yamase").

The hardanger fiddle is featured in the soundtrack of the 2017 film _[Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk\_(2017\_film) "Dunkirk (2017 film)")_, as well as the soundtrack for the 2021 _[Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki\_(TV\_series) "Loki (TV series)")_ series.

[Langeleik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langeleik "Langeleik"), [Scheitholt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheitholt "Scheitholt"), [Epinette des Vosges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epinette_des_Vosges "Epinette des Vosges"), [Dulcimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulcimer "Dulcimer")

The **langspil** (Icelandic pronunciation:[[ˈlauŋkˌspɪːl̥]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Icelandic "Help:IPA/Icelandic"); meaning _long-play_) is a traditional [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland")[drone zither](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_zither "Drone zither"). It has a single melody string and usually 2 [drone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") strings.

The _langspil_ can be played by plucking the strings by hand, with a bow or by hammering. _Langspils_ exist in two basic versions, straight and curved and are generally around the length of 80 cm (31 in), and can be as long as 104 cm (41 in) or as short as 73 cm (29 in). Many different types of wood have traditionally been used, including pine, fir, beechwood, birch, oak and walnut, since they were generally constructed from driftwood.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-auto-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Langspil&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif/lossless-page1-250px-Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif)

[Anna Þórhallsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Þórhallsdóttir (page does not exist)"), wearing a [traditional costume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Ej%C3%B3%C3%B0b%C3%BAningurinn "Þjóðbúningurinn") playing her langspil with a bow

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Langspil_1811.jpg/250px-Langspil_1811.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Langspil_1811.jpg)

Langspil illustration from 1811

The oldest written sources describing the _langspil_ are from the 18th century. In those times _langspil_ instruments are described as a long thin box, wider at the bottom end and with one to six strings. In the early 19th century a version with a curved soundbox emerged which has improved sound qualities. In 1855 the book _Leiðarvísir til að spila á langspil_ (A guide on playing the langspil) was published. It also included information on how to make _langspils_, although with a slight printing error in the fretting. This book increased the popularity of the _langspil_ quite a lot.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-2) However, by the middle of the 20th century the instrument had become rare and few played it any more.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-auto-1)

By the 1960s, the singer [Anna Þórhallsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Þórhallsdóttir (page does not exist)") realized that the _langspil_ was slowly disappearing from Icelandic musical traditions and as a response she spearheaded its revival, which is still ongoing.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-3) Today a number of bands and performers include the _langspil_ in their repertoire, including _Spilmenn Ríkinís_, [Sigurður Rúnar Jónsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigur%C3%B0ur_R%C3%BAnar_J%C3%B3nsson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sigurður Rúnar Jónsson (page does not exist)"), [Bára Grímsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A1ra_Gr%C3%ADmsd%C3%B3ttir "Bára Grímsdóttir"), [Chris Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Foster_(folk_singer) "Chris Foster (folk singer)") and [Þórður Tómasson á Skógum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9E%C3%B3r%C3%B0ur_T%C3%B3masson_%C3%A1_Sk%C3%B3gum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Þórður Tómasson á Skógum (page does not exist)"). The _langspil_ also has an important place in the yearly folk-song festival in [Siglufjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siglufj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Siglufjörður").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-4) In recent years, the singer and music teacher [Eyjólfur Eyjólfsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyj%C3%B3lfur_Eyj%C3%B3lfsson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Eyjólfur Eyjólfsson (page does not exist)") has led a project that aims to teach school children to build and play their own _langspil_ instruments.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-5)

String instrument

Langspil[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Langspil.jpg/250px-Langspil.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Langspil.jpg)

Langspil in the National Museum of Iceland, in Reykjavik, Iceland.
[String instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument")
[Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_instrument_classification "Musical instrument classification")*   [String instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instruments "String instruments")
[Hornbostel–Sachs classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornbostel%E2%80%93Sachs "Hornbostel–Sachs")314.1  
(true board zither)
[Related instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_instrument "Musical instrument")
[Langeleik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langeleik "Langeleik"), [Scheitholt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheitholt "Scheitholt"), [Epinette des Vosges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epinette_des_Vosges "Epinette des Vosges"), [Dulcimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulcimer "Dulcimer")

The **langspil** (Icelandic pronunciation:[[ˈlauŋkˌspɪːl̥]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Icelandic "Help:IPA/Icelandic"); meaning _long-play_) is a traditional [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland")[drone zither](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_zither "Drone zither"). It has a single melody string and usually 2 [drone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") strings.

The _langspil_ can be played by plucking the strings by hand, with a bow or by hammering. _Langspils_ exist in two basic versions, straight and curved and are generally around the length of 80 cm (31 in), and can be as long as 104 cm (41 in) or as short as 73 cm (29 in). Many different types of wood have traditionally been used, including pine, fir, beechwood, birch, oak and walnut, since they were generally constructed from driftwood.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-auto-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Langspil&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif/lossless-page1-250px-Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir_with_Langspil.tif)

[Anna Þórhallsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Þórhallsdóttir (page does not exist)"), wearing a [traditional costume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Ej%C3%B3%C3%B0b%C3%BAningurinn "Þjóðbúningurinn") playing her langspil with a bow

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Langspil_1811.jpg/250px-Langspil_1811.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Langspil_1811.jpg)

Langspil illustration from 1811

The oldest written sources describing the _langspil_ are from the 18th century. In those times _langspil_ instruments are described as a long thin box, wider at the bottom end and with one to six strings. In the early 19th century a version with a curved soundbox emerged which has improved sound qualities. In 1855 the book _Leiðarvísir til að spila á langspil_ (A guide on playing the langspil) was published. It also included information on how to make _langspils_, although with a slight printing error in the fretting. This book increased the popularity of the _langspil_ quite a lot.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-2) However, by the middle of the 20th century the instrument had become rare and few played it any more.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-auto-1)

By the 1960s, the singer [Anna Þórhallsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_%C3%9E%C3%B3rhallsd%C3%B3ttir?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Þórhallsdóttir (page does not exist)") realized that the _langspil_ was slowly disappearing from Icelandic musical traditions and as a response she spearheaded its revival, which is still ongoing.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-3) Today a number of bands and performers include the _langspil_ in their repertoire, including _Spilmenn Ríkinís_, [Sigurður Rúnar Jónsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigur%C3%B0ur_R%C3%BAnar_J%C3%B3nsson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sigurður Rúnar Jónsson (page does not exist)"), [Bára Grímsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A1ra_Gr%C3%ADmsd%C3%B3ttir "Bára Grímsdóttir"), [Chris Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Foster_(folk_singer) "Chris Foster (folk singer)") and [Þórður Tómasson á Skógum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9E%C3%B3r%C3%B0ur_T%C3%B3masson_%C3%A1_Sk%C3%B3gum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Þórður Tómasson á Skógum (page does not exist)"). The _langspil_ also has an important place in the yearly folk-song festival in [Siglufjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siglufj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Siglufjörður").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-4) In recent years, the singer and music teacher [Eyjólfur Eyjólfsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyj%C3%B3lfur_Eyj%C3%B3lfsson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Eyjólfur Eyjólfsson (page does not exist)") has led a project that aims to teach school children to build and play their own _langspil_ instruments.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langspil#cite_note-5)

**Iceland**[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-13) is a [Nordic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_countries "Nordic countries")[island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country") between the [Arctic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean") and the [North Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"), located on the [Mid-Atlantic Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge "Mid-Atlantic Ridge") between [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"). It is Europe's westernmost and most [sparsely populated country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Statice-14) Its capital and largest city is [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk "Reykjavík"), which is home to about 35% of the country's roughly 395,000 residents (excluding nearby towns/suburbs, which are separate municipalities and contribute a further substantial percentage). The official language of the country is [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language"). Iceland is on a [rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift "Rift") between [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_plates "Tectonic plates"), and its geologic activity includes [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser") and frequent [volcanic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_eruptions "Volcanic eruptions").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-15)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-16) The interior consists of a [volcanic plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_plateau "Volcanic plateau") with sand and [lava fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_field "Lava field"), mountains and [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier"), and many [glacial rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_stream "Glacial stream") flow to the sea through the [lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upland_and_lowland "Upland and lowland"). Iceland is warmed by the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") and has a [temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate"), despite being at a latitude just south of the [Arctic Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Circle "Arctic Circle"). Its latitude and marine influence keep summers chilly, and most of its [islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Iceland "List of islands of Iceland") have a [polar climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_climate "Polar climate").

According to the _[Landnámabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landn%C3%A1mab%C3%B3k "Landnámabók")_, an ancient manuscript, the [settlement of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_Iceland "Settlement of Iceland") began in 874 AD, when the [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegians "Norwegians") chieftain [Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") became the island's first permanent settler.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-tomasson-17) In following centuries, Norwegians and to a lesser extent other [Scandinavians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavians "Scandinavians"), migrated to Iceland, bringing with them [thralls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrall "Thrall") (i.e., slaves or serfs) of [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaels "Gaels") origin. The island was governed as an [independent commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth") under the native parliament, the [Althing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althing "Althing"), one of the world's oldest functioning [legislative assemblies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_assemblies "Legislative assemblies"). After a [period of civil strife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs"), Iceland acceded to Norwegian rule in the 13th century. In 1397, Iceland followed [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway")'s integration into the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") along with the kingdoms of [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"), coming under _de facto_[Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes "Danes") rule upon its dissolution in 1523. The Danish kingdom introduced [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") by force in 1550,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-18) and the [Treaty of Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Kiel "Treaty of Kiel") formally ceded Iceland to Denmark in 1814.

[Influenced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence_of_the_French_Revolution "Influence of the French Revolution") by ideals of [nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalism "Nationalism") after the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), Iceland's [struggle for independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_independence_movement "Icelandic independence movement") took shape, culminating with the [Danish–Icelandic Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Act_of_Union "Danish–Icelandic Act of Union") in 1918, and the establishment of the [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"), sharing through a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") the incumbent [monarch of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch_of_Denmark "Monarch of Denmark"). During the [occupation of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_Denmark "Occupation of Denmark") in World War II, Iceland voted overwhelmingly to [become a republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Icelandic_constitutional_referendum "1944 Icelandic constitutional referendum") in 1944, ending its remaining formal ties to Denmark. Although the Althing was suspended from 1799 to 1845, Iceland nevertheless has a claim to sustaining one of the world's longest-running parliaments. Until the 20th century, Iceland relied largely on [subsistence fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsistence_fishing "Subsistence fishing") and agriculture. Industrialisation of the fisheries and [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan "Marshall Plan") aid after World War II brought prosperity, and Iceland became one of the world's wealthiest and most developed nations. In 1950, Iceland joined the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-19) In 1994 it became a part of the [European Economic Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Area "European Economic Area"), further diversifying [its economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Iceland "Economy of Iceland") into sectors such as finance, biotechnology, and [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing_in_Iceland "Manufacturing in Iceland").

Iceland has a [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy") with relatively low [taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Iceland "Taxation in Iceland"), compared to other [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") countries,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-20) as well as the [highest trade union membership in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_union#Prevalence_worldwide "Trade union").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-ILO_Density-21) It maintains a [Nordic social welfare system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_model "Nordic model") that provides [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") and [tertiary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education "Tertiary education").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-22)[Iceland ranks highly in international comparisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_rankings_of_Iceland "International rankings of Iceland") of national performance, such as quality of life, education, protection of civil liberties, government transparency, and economic freedom. It has the smallest population of any [NATO member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_member "NATO member") and is the only one with [no standing army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_without_armed_forces "List of sovereign states without armed forces"), possessing only a lightly armed [coast guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Coast_Guard "Icelandic Coast Guard").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-23)

## Etymology

See also: [Names of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Iceland "Names of Iceland")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg/250px-Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg)

Norsemen landing in Iceland – a 19th-century depiction by [Oscar Wergeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wergeland "Oscar Wergeland")

The _Landnámabók_ names [Naddodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naddodd "Naddodd") ([Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): _Naddoðr_) as the first [Norseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norseman "Norseman") to reach Iceland in the ninth century, having gotten lost while sailing from Norway to the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands"). He gave the island its first name of _Snæland_ (English: _Snowland_). The second explorer to arrive was the Swedish [Garðar Svavarsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gar%C3%B0ar_Svavarsson "Garðar Svavarsson"), who circumnavigated the island and named it _Garðarshólmur_ (English: _Garðar's Isle_) after himself.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-24)

The island's present name originated from [Flóki Vilgerðarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fl%C3%B3ki_Vilger%C3%B0arson "Flóki Vilgerðarson"), the first Norseman to intentionally travel to Iceland. According to the [Sagas of Icelanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagas_of_Icelanders "Sagas of Icelanders"), Flóki coined the name after he climbed a mountain, despondent after a harsh winter in present-day [Vatnsfjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatnsfj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Vatnsfjörður"), and saw an [ice cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_cap "Ice cap").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Evans-25) The notion that Iceland's settlers chose that name to discourage competing settlements is most likely a myth.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Evans-25)
