[Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") (modern Icelandic: _Ingólfur Arnarson_), the first permanent Scandinavian settler

According to both _[Landnámabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landn%C3%A1mab%C3%B3k "Landnámabók")_ and _[Íslendingabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Dslendingab%C3%B3k "Íslendingabók")_, monks known as the [Papar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papar "Papar") lived in Iceland before Scandinavian settlers arrived, possibly members of a [Hiberno-Scottish mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiberno-Scottish_mission "Hiberno-Scottish mission"). An archaeological excavation has revealed the ruins of a cabin in [Hafnir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnir "Hafnir") on the [Reykjanes peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjanes_peninsula "Reykjanes peninsula"). [Carbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dating "Carbon dating") indicates that it was abandoned sometime between 770 and 880.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-26) In 2016, archaeologists uncovered a [longhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longhouse "Longhouse") in [Stöðvarfjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%B6%C3%B0varfj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Stöðvarfjörður") that may date to as early as 800.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-27)

Swedish Viking explorer [Garðar Svavarsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gar%C3%B0ar_Svavarsson "Garðar Svavarsson") was the first to circumnavigate Iceland in 870, and established that it was an island.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-28) He stayed during the winter and built a house in [Húsavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%BAsav%C3%ADk "Húsavík"). Garðar departed the following summer, but one of his men, [Náttfari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A1ttfari "Náttfari"), decided to stay behind with two slaves. Náttfari settled in what is now known as Náttfaravík, and he and his slaves became the first documented permanent residents of Iceland.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-30)

The Norwegian-Norse chieftain [Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") built his homestead in present-day [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk "Reykjavík") in 874. Ingólfr was followed by many other emigrant settlers, largely Scandinavians and their [thralls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrall "Thrall"), many of whom were [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") or [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-31) By 930, most [arable land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arable_land "Arable land") on the island had been claimed; the [Althing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althing "Althing"), a legislative and judicial assembly, was initiated to regulate the [Icelandic Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth"). The lack of arable land also served as an impetus to the [settlement of Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_settlements_in_Greenland "Norse settlements in Greenland") starting in 986.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-32) The period of these early settlements coincided with the [Medieval Warm Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Warm_Period "Medieval Warm Period"), when temperatures were similar to those of the early 20th century.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-33) At that time, about 25% of Iceland was covered with forest, compared to 1% in the present day.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-34)[Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") was adopted [by consensus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianisation_of_Iceland "Christianisation of Iceland") around 999–1000, although [Norse paganism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_paganism "Norse paganism") persisted among segments of the population for some years afterward.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-35)

### Iceland as a possession

#### Middle Ages

See also: [Age of the Sturlungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg/250px-Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg)

[Turf houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_turf_house "Icelandic turf house") have been constructed since Iceland was settled in the 9th century.

The [Icelandic Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth"), established in the 10th century, faced internal strife during the [Age of the Sturlungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs") (c. 1220–1264). This period was marked by violent conflicts among chieftains, notably the Sturlung family, leading to the weakening of the Commonwealth's political structure.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-36) The culmination of the struggles was the signing of the Old Covenant ([Gamli sáttmáli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamli_s%C3%A1ttm%C3%A1li "Gamli sáttmáli")) in 1262–1264, bringing [Iceland under Norwegian rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland "History of Iceland").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-37)

Environmental challenges further impacted [medieval Icelandic society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland "History of Iceland").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-38) Upon settlement, approximately 25–40% of Iceland was forested. However, extensive deforestation occurred as forests were cleared for timber, firewood, and to create grazing land for livestock. This led to significant soil erosion and a decline in arable land, exacerbating the difficulties of sustaining agriculture in Iceland's harsh climate.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-39) Agriculture during this period was predominantly pastoral, focusing on livestock such as sheep, cattle, and horses. While early settlers cultivated barley, the cooling climate from the 12th century onwards made grain cultivation increasingly difficult. The [Little Ice Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age "Little Ice Age") began around 1300, bringing colder and more unpredictable weather, further shortening growing seasons and making farming more challenging.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-40)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-41)

The [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") reached Iceland in 1402–1404 and again in 1494–1495, with devastating effects.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-42) The first outbreak is estimated to have killed 50–60% of the population, while the second resulted in a 30–50% mortality rate. These pandemics significantly reduced the population, leading to social and economic disruptions.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-43)

In 1380, after the death of [Haakon VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haakon_VI "Haakon VI"), his son [Olaf II of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olaf_II_of_Denmark "Olaf II of Denmark") succeeded to the Norwegian throne, uniting the crowns of Denmark and Norway under one monarch. Because Iceland was part of the Norwegian realm, it thereby came under the Danish-Norwegian crown. In 1397, the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") brought Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-45)

#### Reformation and the Early Modern period

See also: [Icelandic Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Reformation "Icelandic Reformation"), [Danish trade monopoly in Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_trade_monopoly_in_Iceland "Danish trade monopoly in Iceland"), and [Móðuharðindin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B3%C3%B0uhar%C3%B0indin "Móðuharðindin")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Bolungarvik_02.jpg/250px-Bolungarvik_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bolungarvik_02.jpg)

_Ósvör_, a replica of an old fishing outpost outside [Bolungarvík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolungarv%C3%ADk "Bolungarvík")

Around the middle of the 16th century, as part of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation"), King [Christian III of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_III_of_Denmark "Christian III of Denmark") began to impose [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") on all his subjects. [Jón Arason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3n_Arason "Jón Arason"), the last Icelandic Catholic bishop, and two of his sons were beheaded in 1550. Iceland then became officially Lutheran, and Lutheranism has since remained the dominant religion.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas%2C_sive%2C_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_%2824696368309%29.jpg/250px-Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas%2C_sive%2C_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_%2824696368309%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas,_sive,_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_(24696368309).jpg)

A map of Iceland published in the early 17th century by [Gerardus Mercator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerardus_Mercator "Gerardus Mercator")

In the 17th and 18th centuries, Denmark imposed [harsh trade restrictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Trade_Monopoly "Danish–Icelandic Trade Monopoly") on Iceland. Natural disasters, including volcanic eruptions and disease, contributed to a decreasing population. In the summer of 1627, [Barbary Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_Pirates "Barbary Pirates") committed the events known locally as the [Turkish Abductions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Abductions "Turkish Abductions"), in which hundreds of residents were taken into slavery in North Africa and dozens killed; this was the only invasion in Icelandic history to have caused casualties.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-46)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-47) The [1707–08 Iceland smallpox epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1707%E2%80%9308_Iceland_smallpox_epidemic "1707–08 Iceland smallpox epidemic") is estimated to have killed a quarter to a third of the population.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-48)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-49) In 1783 the [Laki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki "Laki") volcano erupted, with devastating effects.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-50) In the years following the eruption, known as the [Mist Hardships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mist_Hardships "Mist Hardships") ([Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language"): _Móðuharðindin_), over half of all livestock in the country died. Around a quarter of the population starved to death in the ensuing [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-51)

#### 1814–1918: independence movement

See also: [Icelandic independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_independence_movement "Icelandic independence movement") and [Fjölnir (journal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fj%C3%B6lnir_(journal) "Fjölnir (journal)")

After the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars") in 1814, Denmark-Norway broke up into two separate kingdoms under the [Treaty of Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Kiel "Treaty of Kiel"), but Iceland remained a Danish dependency. Throughout the 19th century, the country's climate continued to grow colder, resulting in mass emigration to the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World"), particularly to the region of [Gimli, Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimli,_Manitoba "Gimli, Manitoba") in Canada, which was sometimes referred to as [New Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Iceland "New Iceland"). About 15,000 people emigrated out of a total population of 70,000.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-52)

A national consciousness arose in the first half of the 19th century, inspired by [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") and [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist "Nationalist") ideas from mainland Europe. An Icelandic independence movement took shape in the 1850s under the leadership of [Jón Sigurðsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3n_Sigur%C3%B0sson "Jón Sigurðsson"), based on the burgeoning Icelandic nationalism inspired by the _[Fjölnismenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fj%C3%B6lnismenn "Fjölnismenn")_ and other Danish-educated Icelandic intellectuals. In 1874, poet and clergyman [Matthías Jochumsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matth%C3%ADas_Jochumsson "Matthías Jochumsson") wrote the lyrics of "[Lofsöngur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lofs%C3%B6ngur "Lofsöngur")", which became the Icelandic [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem "National anthem"). Composer [Sveinbjörn Sveinbjörnsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveinbj%C3%B6rn_Sveinbj%C3%B6rnsson "Sveinbjörn Sveinbjörnsson") wrote the music.

In 1874, Denmark granted Iceland a constitution and limited home rule. That was expanded in 1904, and [Hannes Hafstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Hafstein "Hannes Hafstein") served as the first [Minister for Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Iceland "Minister for Iceland") in the Danish cabinet.

### 1918–1944: independence and the Kingdom of Iceland

See also: [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"), [Invasion of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Iceland "Invasion of Iceland"), and [Iceland in World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_in_World_War_II "Iceland in World War II")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/HMS_Berwick_%2865%29.jpg/250px-HMS_Berwick_%2865%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HMS_Berwick_(65).jpg)

[HMS _Berwick_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Berwick_(65) "HMS Berwick (65)") led the British [invasion of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Iceland "Invasion of Iceland").

The [Danish–Icelandic Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Act_of_Union "Danish–Icelandic Act of Union"), an agreement with Denmark signed on 1 December 1918 and valid for 25 years, recognised Iceland as a fully sovereign and independent state in a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") with Denmark. The Government of Iceland established an embassy in Copenhagen and requested that Denmark carry out on its behalf certain defence and foreign affairs matters, subject to consultation with the Althing. Danish embassies around the world displayed two coats of arms and two flags: those of the Kingdom of Denmark and those of the [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"). Iceland's legal position became comparable to those of countries belonging to the Commonwealth of Nations, such as Canada, whose sovereign is King [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III").

During World War II, Iceland joined Denmark in asserting neutrality. After the [German occupation of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_occupation_of_Denmark "German occupation of Denmark") on 9 April 1940, the Althing replaced the king with a regent and declared that the Icelandic government would take control of its own defence and foreign affairs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-:0-53) A month later, British armed forces conducted [Operation Fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Fork "Operation Fork"), the invasion and occupation of the country, violating Icelandic [neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrality_(international_relations) "Neutrality (international relations)").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-54) In 1941, the Government of Iceland, friendly to Britain, invited the United States, then neutral, to take over its defence so that Britain could use its troops elsewhere.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-:0-53)

### 1944–present: Republic of Iceland

See also: [Icelandic constitutional referendum, 1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_constitutional_referendum,_1944 "Icelandic constitutional referendum, 1944"); [Iceland in the Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_in_the_Cold_War "Iceland in the Cold War"); and [Cod Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_Wars "Cod Wars")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Scylla-Odinn.jpg/250px-Scylla-Odinn.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scylla-Odinn.jpg)

A British warship, [HMS _Scylla_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Scylla_(F71) "HMS Scylla (F71)") (right), collides with Icelandic coast guard vessel [ICGV _Óðinn_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICGV_%C3%93%C3%B0inn "ICGV Óðinn") in the Atlantic Ocean during the [Third Cod War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_Wars "Cod Wars").

On 31 December 1943, the [Danish–Icelandic Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Act_of_Union "Danish–Icelandic Act of Union") expired after 25 years. Beginning on 20 May 1944, Icelanders voted in a four-day plebiscite on whether to terminate the personal union with Denmark, abolish the monarchy, and establish a republic. The vote was 97% to end the union, and 95% in favour of the new republican constitution.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-55) Iceland formally became a republic on 17 June 1944, with [Sveinn Björnsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveinn_Bj%C3%B6rnsson "Sveinn Björnsson") as its first president.

In 1946, the US Defense Force left Iceland. The nation formally became a member of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") on 30 March 1949, amid [domestic controversy and riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_anti-NATO_riot_in_Iceland "1949 anti-NATO riot in Iceland"). On 5 May 1951, a defence agreement was signed with the United States. American troops returned to Iceland as the [Iceland Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_Defence_Force "Iceland Defence Force") and remained throughout the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"). The US withdrew the last of its forces on 30 September 2006.

Iceland prospered during the Second World War. The immediate post-war period was followed by substantial [economic growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_growth "Economic growth"), driven by the industrialisation of the fishing industry and the US [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan "Marshall Plan") program, through which Icelanders received the most aid per capita of any European country (at US$209, with war-ravaged [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") a distant second at US$109).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-56)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-57)[Vigdís Finnbogadóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigd%C3%ADs_Finnbogad%C3%B3ttir "Vigdís Finnbogadóttir") assumed Iceland's presidency on 1 August 1980, making her the first elected female head of state in the world.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-58)

The 1970s were marked by the [Cod Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cod_Wars "Cod Wars"), which were several disputes with the United Kingdom over Iceland's extension of its fishing limits to 200 nmi (370 km) offshore. Iceland hosted a [summit in Reykjavík in 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk_Summit "Reykjavík Summit") between United States President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") and Soviet Premier [Mikhail Gorbachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev "Mikhail Gorbachev"), during which they took significant steps towards [nuclear disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament"). A few years later, Iceland became the first country to recognise the independence of [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia "Estonia"), [Latvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia "Latvia"), and [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") as they [broke away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union "Dissolution of the Soviet Union") from the [USSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR "USSR"). Throughout the 1990s, the country expanded its international role and developed a foreign policy oriented towards humanitarian and peacekeeping causes. To that end, Iceland provided aid and expertise to various NATO-led interventions in [Bosnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"), [Kosovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_War "Kosovo War"), and [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-59)

Iceland joined the [European Economic Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Area "European Economic Area") in 1994, after which the economy was greatly diversified and liberalised. International economic relations increased further after 2001 when Iceland's newly deregulated banks began to raise great amounts of [external debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_debt "External debt"), contributing to a 32 per cent increase in Iceland's [gross national income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_national_income "Gross national income") between 2002 and 2007.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-jackson-60)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-61)

#### Economic boom and crisis

Further information: [2008–2011 Icelandic financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008%E2%80%932011_Icelandic_financial_crisis "2008–2011 Icelandic financial crisis") and [2009 Icelandic financial crisis protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Icelandic_financial_crisis_protests "2009 Icelandic financial crisis protests")

In 2003–2007, after the privatisation of the banking sector under the government of [Davíð Oddsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dav%C3%AD%C3%B0_Oddsson "Davíð Oddsson"), Iceland moved towards having an economy based on international investment banking and financial services.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Lewis-62) It was quickly becoming one of the most prosperous countries in the world, but was hit hard by a [major financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008%E2%80%932011_Icelandic_financial_crisis "2008–2011 Icelandic financial crisis").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Lewis-62) The crisis resulted in the greatest migration from Iceland since 1887, with a net emigration of 5,000 people in 2009.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-nordregio.se-63)

#### Since 2012

Iceland's economy stabilised under the government of [Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3hanna_Sigur%C3%B0ard%C3%B3ttir "Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir"), growing by 1.6% in 2012.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-64) The centre-right [Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_(Iceland) "Independence Party (Iceland)") was returned to power in coalition with the [Progressive Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Party_(Iceland) "Progressive Party (Iceland)") in the 2013 election.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-65) In the following years, Iceland benefited from a surge in tourism as the country became a popular holiday destination. In 2016, Prime Minister [Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmundur_Dav%C3%AD%C3%B0_Gunnlaugsson "Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson") resigned after being implicated in the [Panama Papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Papers "Panama Papers") scandal.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-66) Early elections in 2016 resulted in a right-wing coalition government of the [Independence Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_(Iceland) "Independence Party (Iceland)"), [Viðreisn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vi%C3%B0reisn "Viðreisn") and [Bright Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bright_Future_(Iceland) "Bright Future (Iceland)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-67) This government fell when Bright Future quit the coalition due to a scandal involving a letter of support for a convicted child sex offender from the father of Prime Minister [Bjarni Benediktsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bjarni_Benediktsson_(born_1970) "Bjarni Benediktsson (born 1970)") of the Indepedence Party.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-68)[Snap elections in October 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Icelandic_parliamentary_election "2017 Icelandic parliamentary election") brought to power a new coalition consisting of the Independence Party, the Progressive Party, and the [Left-Green Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-Green_Movement "Left-Green Movement"), headed by [Katrín Jakobsdóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katr%C3%ADn_Jakobsd%C3%B3ttir "Katrín Jakobsdóttir").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-69)

After the 2021 parliamentary [election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Icelandic_parliamentary_election "2021 Icelandic parliamentary election"), the new government was, just like the previous government, a tri-party coalition of the Independence Party, the Progressive Party, and the Left-Green Movement, headed by Prime Minister Katrín Jakobsdóttir.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-70) In April 2024, Bjarni Benediktsson succeeded Katrín as prime minister.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-71) In a [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Icelandic_parliamentary_election "2024 Icelandic parliamentary election") in November 2024, the centre-left [Social Democratic Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Alliance "Social Democratic Alliance") became the biggest party, and Social Democrat [Kristrún Frostadóttir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristr%C3%BAn_Frostad%C3%B3ttir "Kristrún Frostadóttir") became the next Prime Minister of Iceland.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-72)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Iceland "Geography of Iceland")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Map_of_Iceland.svg/500px-Map_of_Iceland.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Iceland.svg)

General topographic map

Iceland is at the juncture of the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean. The main island is entirely south of the [Arctic Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Circle "Arctic Circle"), which passes through the small Icelandic island of [Grímsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%ADmsey "Grímsey") off the main island's northern coast. The country lies between latitudes [63](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circles_of_latitude_between_the_60th_parallel_north_and_the_65th_parallel_north#63rd_parallel_north "Circles of latitude between the 60th parallel north and the 65th parallel north") and [68°N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/68%C2%B0N "68°N"), and longitudes [25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_meridian_west "25th meridian west") and [13°W](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_meridian_west "13th meridian west").

Iceland is closer to [continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe") than to mainland North America, although it is closest to [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), an island of North America. Iceland is generally included in Europe for geographical, historical, political, cultural, linguistic, and practical reasons.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Ingebritsen2000-73)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-LehtiSmith2003-74)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Miles2005-75)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Dhondt2011-76) Geologically, the island includes parts of both continental plates. The closest bodies of land in Europe are the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands") (420 km; 225 nmi); [Jan Mayen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Mayen "Jan Mayen") Island (570 km; 310 nmi); [Shetland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shetland "Shetland") and the [Outer Hebrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides "Outer Hebrides"), both about 740 km (400 nmi); and the Scottish mainland and [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney "Orkney"), both about 750 km (405 nmi). The nearest part of Continental Europe is mainland Norway, about 970 km (525 nmi) away, while mainland North America is 2,070 km (1,120 nmi) away, at the northern tip of [Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador "Labrador").

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Icelandic_landscapes.jpg/250px-Icelandic_landscapes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Icelandic_landscapes.jpg)

Three typical Icelandic landscapes

Iceland is the [18th-largest island in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_by_area "List of islands by area"), and the second-largest island in Europe, smaller than Great Britain and bigger than Ireland.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-77) The main island covers 101,826 km 2 (39,315 sq mi), but the entire country is 103,000 km 2 (40,000 sq mi) in size, of which 62.7% is [tundra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra "Tundra"). Iceland contains about 30 minor islands, including the lightly populated Grímsey and the [Vestmannaeyjar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestmannaeyjar "Vestmannaeyjar") archipelago. Lakes and glaciers cover 14.3% of its surface; only 23% is vegetated.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-NLS-78) The largest lakes are [Þórisvatn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9E%C3%B3risvatn "Þórisvatn") reservoir: 83–88 km 2 (32–34 sq mi) and [Þingvallavatn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Eingvallavatn "Þingvallavatn"): 82 km 2 (32 sq mi); other important lakes include [Lagarfljót](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagarflj%C3%B3t "Lagarfljót") and [Mývatn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BDvatn "Mývatn"). [Jökulsárlón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6kuls%C3%A1rl%C3%B3n "Jökulsárlón") is the deepest lake, at 248 m (814 ft).[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-79) Geologically, Iceland is a part of the [Mid-Atlantic Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge "Mid-Atlantic Ridge"), a ridge along which the [oceanic crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_crust "Oceanic crust") spreads and forms new crust. This part of the mid-ocean ridge is located above a [mantle plume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantle_plume "Mantle plume"), causing Iceland to be [subaerial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subaerial "Subaerial") (above the surface of the sea). The ridge marks the boundary between the [Eurasian Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Plate "Eurasian Plate") and the [North American Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Plate "North American Plate"), and Iceland was created by [rifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift "Rift") and [accretion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accretion_(geology) "Accretion (geology)") through volcanism along the ridge.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-80)

Many [fjords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord "Fjord") punctuate Iceland's 4,970-kilometre-long (3,090 mi) coastline, which is also where most settlements are situated. The island's interior, the [Highlands of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlands_of_Iceland "Highlands of Iceland"), is a cold and uninhabitable combination of sand, mountains, and [lava fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_field "Lava field"). The major towns are the capital city of [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk "Reykjavík"), along with its outlying towns of [Kópavogur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B3pavogur "Kópavogur"), [Hafnarfjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnarfj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Hafnarfjörður"), and [Garðabær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gar%C3%B0ab%C3%A6r "Garðabær"), nearby [Reykjanesbær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjanesb%C3%A6r "Reykjanesbær") where the international airport is located, and the town of [Akureyri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akureyri "Akureyri") in northern Iceland. The island of Grímsey on the Arctic Circle contains the northernmost habitation of Iceland, whereas [Kolbeinsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolbeinsey "Kolbeinsey") contains the northernmost point of Iceland.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-CIA_Govt-81) Iceland has [three national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_Iceland "List of national parks of Iceland"): [Vatnajökull National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatnaj%C3%B6kull_National_Park "Vatnajökull National Park"), [Snæfellsjökull National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sn%C3%A6fellsj%C3%B6kull_National_Park "Snæfellsjökull National Park"), and [Þingvellir National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Eingvellir_National_Park "Þingvellir National Park").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-82) The country is considered a "strong performer" in environmental protection.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-83)

### Geology

Main article: [Geology of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Iceland "Geology of Iceland")

Further information: [Iceland hotspot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_hotspot "Iceland hotspot")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Erupting_geysir.jpg/250px-Erupting_geysir.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erupting_geysir.jpg)

[Geysir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geysir "Geysir") which is in [Haukadalur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haukadalur_(Bl%C3%A1sk%C3%B3gabygg%C3%B0) "Haukadalur (Bláskógabyggð)") valley, is shown erupting. It is the oldest known [geyser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser") in the world.

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Iceland_-_2017-02-22_-_Gullfoss_-_3677.jpg/250px-Iceland_-_2017-02-22_-_Gullfoss_-_3677.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iceland_-_2017-02-22_-_Gullfoss_-_3677.jpg)

[Gullfoss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gullfoss "Gullfoss"), an iconic waterfall of Iceland

Iceland is the only large [insular landmass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island "Island") in the world which is located on a [mid-ocean ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-ocean_ridge "Mid-ocean ridge") above sea level. It is probably the only place in the world where the effects of two [major tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tectonic_plates#Major_plates "List of tectonic plates") drifting apart can easily be observed above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). The island sits directly on the [Mid-Atlantic Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge "Mid-Atlantic Ridge"), where the [Eurasian Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Plate "Eurasian Plate") and the [North American Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Plate "North American Plate") are moving away from each other.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-84)

A geologically young land at 16 to 18 million years old, Iceland is the surface expression of the [Iceland Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_Plateau "Iceland Plateau"), a [large igneous province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_igneous_province "Large igneous province") forming as a result of volcanism from the [Iceland hotspot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_hotspot "Iceland hotspot") and along the [Mid-Atlantic Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge "Mid-Atlantic Ridge"), the latter of which runs right through it.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-85)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-86) This means that the island is highly geologically active with many volcanoes including [Hekla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hekla "Hekla"), [Eldgjá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldgj%C3%A1 "Eldgjá"), [Herðubreið](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her%C3%B0ubrei%C3%B0 "Herðubreið"), and [Eldfell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell "Eldfell").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-87) The volcanic eruption of [Laki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki "Laki") in 1783–1784 caused a famine that killed nearly a quarter of the island's population.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-88) In addition, the eruption caused dust clouds and haze to appear over most of Europe and parts of Africa and Asia for several months afterwards, and affected climates in other areas.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-89)

Iceland has many [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser"), including [Geysir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geysir "Geysir"), from which the English word is derived, and the famous [Strokkur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strokkur "Strokkur"), which erupts every 8–10 minutes. After a phase of inactivity, Geysir started erupting again after [a series of earthquakes in 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Iceland_earthquakes "2000 Iceland earthquakes"). Geysir has since grown quieter and does not erupt often.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-90)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Geleira_S%C3%B3lheimaj%C3%B6kull.jpg/250px-Geleira_S%C3%B3lheimaj%C3%B6kull.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Geleira_S%C3%B3lheimaj%C3%B6kull.jpg)

[Sólheimajökull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%B3lheimaj%C3%B6kull "Sólheimajökull") glacier

With the widespread availability of [geothermal power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power "Geothermal power") and the harnessing of many rivers and waterfalls for [hydroelectricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroelectricity "Hydroelectricity"), most residents have access to inexpensive hot water, heating, and electricity. The island is composed primarily of [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt "Basalt"), a low-[silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silica "Silica") lava associated with [effusive volcanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effusive_volcanism "Effusive volcanism"), as has also occurred in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"). Iceland, however, has a variety of volcanic types (composite and fissure), many producing more evolved lavas such as [rhyolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyolite "Rhyolite") and [andesite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andesite "Andesite").

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Eyjafjallajokull-April-17.JPG/250px-Eyjafjallajokull-April-17.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eyjafjallajokull-April-17.JPG)

The [eruption of Eyjafjallajökull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_eruptions_of_Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull "2010 eruptions of Eyjafjallajökull")

[Surtsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surtsey "Surtsey"), one of the youngest islands in the world, is part of Iceland. Named after [Surtr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surtr "Surtr"), it rose above the ocean in a series of volcanic eruptions between 8 November 1963 and 5 June 1968.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-CIA_Govt-81) Only scientists researching the growth of new life are allowed to visit the island.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-91) Iceland has hundreds of volcanoes with about 30 [active volcanic systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland "Volcanism of Iceland").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-92) Within each are volcano-tectonic fissure systems, and many, but not all of them, also have at least one [central volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_volcano "Central volcano") (mostly in the form of a [stratovolcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratovolcano "Stratovolcano"), sometimes of a [shield volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shield_volcano "Shield volcano") with a [magma chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma_chamber "Magma chamber") underneath). Several classifications of the systems exist, for example there is one with 30 systems,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Andrews2008-93):10 and one with 34 systems, with the latter currently being used in Iceland itself.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-EIV-94)

### Climate

Main articles: [Climate of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Iceland "Climate of Iceland") and [Tornadoes in Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_in_Iceland "Tornadoes in Iceland")

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Iceland_K%C3%B6ppen.svg/250px-Iceland_K%C3%B6ppen.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iceland_K%C3%B6ppen.svg)

[Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification") types of Iceland

The climate of Iceland's coast is [subarctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subarctic_climate "Subarctic climate"). The warm [North Atlantic Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current "North Atlantic Current") ensures generally higher annual temperatures than in most places of similar latitude in the world. Regions in the world with similar climates include the [Aleutian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleutian_Islands "Aleutian Islands"), the [Alaska Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Peninsula "Alaska Peninsula"), and [Tierra del Fuego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tierra_del_Fuego "Tierra del Fuego"), although these regions are closer to the equator. Despite its proximity to the Arctic, the island's coasts remain ice-free through the winter. Ice incursions are rare, with the last having occurred on the north coast in 1969.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-95)

The climate varies between different parts of the island. Generally speaking, the south coast is warmer, wetter, and windier than the north. The Central Highlands are the coldest part of the country. Low-lying inland areas in the north are the aridest. Snowfall in winter is more common in the north than in the south. The highest air temperature recorded was 30.5°C (86.9°F) on 22 June 1939 at Teigarhorn on the southeastern coast. The lowest was −38°C (−36.4°F) on 22 January 1918 at Grímsstaðir and Möðrudalur in the northeastern hinterland. The temperature records for Reykjavík are 26.2°C (79.2°F) on 30 July 2008, and −24.5°C (−12.1°F) on 21 January 1918.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Due to [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), Iceland is experiencing faster [glacial retreat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_retreat "Glacial retreat"), changing vegetation patterns, and shifting marine ecosystems.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-96) Iceland's retreating glaciers have global and local consequences. Melting of Iceland's glaciers could raise sea levels by one centimeter (0.39 in),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-:22-97) which could lead to erosion and flooding worldwide.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-98) In late 2025, Iceland elevated the potential [collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abrupt_climate_change "Abrupt climate change") of the [Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Meridional_Overturning_Circulation "Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation") (AMOC) to a national security risk, recognising severe climate impacts like extreme European winters, food/energy insecurity, and economic disruption as major threats.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-99)

### Wildlife

Main article: [Wildlife of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife_of_Iceland "Wildlife of Iceland")

The entire country is in a single [ecoregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecoregion "Ecoregion"), the [Iceland boreal birch forests and alpine tundra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_boreal_birch_forests_and_alpine_tundra "Iceland boreal birch forests and alpine tundra"). Some areas are covered by [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier").

#### Plants

[Phytogeographically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytogeographically "Phytogeographically"), Iceland belongs to the Arctic province of the [Circumboreal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumboreal_Region "Circumboreal Region") within the [Boreal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boreal_Kingdom "Boreal Kingdom"). Vegetation is dominated by grasslands, which are regularly grazed by livestock. The most common native tree is the northern birch (_[Betula pubescens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betula\_pubescens "Betula pubescens")_), which historically formed extensive forests across Iceland, along with aspens (_[Populus tremula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populus\_tremula "Populus tremula")_), rowans (_[Sorbus aucuparia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbus\_aucuparia "Sorbus aucuparia")_), the only native [gymnosperm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnosperm "Gymnosperm"), common juniper (_[Juniperus communis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juniperus\_communis "Juniperus communis")_),[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-100) and other smaller trees, mainly willows (Salix spp.).

When the island was first settled, it was extensively forested, with around 30% of the land covered in trees. In the late 12th century, [Ari the Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ari_the_Wise "Ari the Wise") described it in the [Íslendingabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Dslendingab%C3%B3k "Íslendingabók") as "forested from mountain to sea shore".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Dirt-101) Permanent human settlement greatly disturbed the isolated ecosystem of thin, volcanic soils and limited [species diversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_richness "Species richness"). The forests were heavily exploited over the centuries for firewood and timber.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-wildlife-102)[Deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation"), climatic deterioration during the [Little Ice Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age "Little Ice Age"), and overgrazing by sheep imported by settlers caused a loss of critical topsoil due to [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion "Erosion"). **Iceland**[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-13) is a [Nordic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_countries "Nordic countries")[island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country") between the [Arctic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean") and the [North Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"), located on the [Mid-Atlantic Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge "Mid-Atlantic Ridge") between [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"). It is Europe's westernmost and most [sparsely populated country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Statice-14) Its capital and largest city is [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk "Reykjavík"), which is home to about 35% of the country's roughly 395,000 residents (excluding nearby towns/suburbs, which are separate municipalities and contribute a further substantial percentage). The official language of the country is [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language"). Iceland is on a [rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift "Rift") between [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_plates "Tectonic plates"), and its geologic activity includes [geysers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geyser "Geyser") and frequent [volcanic eruptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_eruptions "Volcanic eruptions").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-15)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-16) The interior consists of a [volcanic plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_plateau "Volcanic plateau") with sand and [lava fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava_field "Lava field"), mountains and [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier"), and many [glacial rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_stream "Glacial stream") flow to the sea through the [lowlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upland_and_lowland "Upland and lowland"). Iceland is warmed by the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") and has a [temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate"), despite being at a latitude just south of the [Arctic Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Circle "Arctic Circle"). Its latitude and marine influence keep summers chilly, and most of its [islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Iceland "List of islands of Iceland") have a [polar climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_climate "Polar climate").

According to the _[Landnámabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landn%C3%A1mab%C3%B3k "Landnámabók")_, an ancient manuscript, the [settlement of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_Iceland "Settlement of Iceland") began in 874 AD, when the [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegians "Norwegians") chieftain [Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") became the island's first permanent settler.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-tomasson-17) In following centuries, Norwegians and to a lesser extent other [Scandinavians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavians "Scandinavians"), migrated to Iceland, bringing with them [thralls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrall "Thrall") (i.e., slaves or serfs) of [Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaels "Gaels") origin. The island was governed as an [independent commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth") under the native parliament, the [Althing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althing "Althing"), one of the world's oldest functioning [legislative assemblies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_assemblies "Legislative assemblies"). After a [period of civil strife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs"), Iceland acceded to Norwegian rule in the 13th century. In 1397, Iceland followed [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway")'s integration into the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") along with the kingdoms of [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"), coming under _de facto_[Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes "Danes") rule upon its dissolution in 1523. The Danish kingdom introduced [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") by force in 1550,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-18) and the [Treaty of Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Kiel "Treaty of Kiel") formally ceded Iceland to Denmark in 1814.

[Influenced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influence_of_the_French_Revolution "Influence of the French Revolution") by ideals of [nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalism "Nationalism") after the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), Iceland's [struggle for independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_independence_movement "Icelandic independence movement") took shape, culminating with the [Danish–Icelandic Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Act_of_Union "Danish–Icelandic Act of Union") in 1918, and the establishment of the [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"), sharing through a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") the incumbent [monarch of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch_of_Denmark "Monarch of Denmark"). During the [occupation of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_Denmark "Occupation of Denmark") in World War II, Iceland voted overwhelmingly to [become a republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Icelandic_constitutional_referendum "1944 Icelandic constitutional referendum") in 1944, ending its remaining formal ties to Denmark. Although the Althing was suspended from 1799 to 1845, Iceland nevertheless has a claim to sustaining one of the world's longest-running parliaments. Until the 20th century, Iceland relied largely on [subsistence fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsistence_fishing "Subsistence fishing") and agriculture. Industrialisation of the fisheries and [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan "Marshall Plan") aid after World War II brought prosperity, and Iceland became one of the world's wealthiest and most developed nations. In 1950, Iceland joined the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-19) In 1994 it became a part of the [European Economic Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Area "European Economic Area"), further diversifying [its economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Iceland "Economy of Iceland") into sectors such as finance, biotechnology, and [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing_in_Iceland "Manufacturing in Iceland").

Iceland has a [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy") with relatively low [taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Iceland "Taxation in Iceland"), compared to other [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") countries,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-20) as well as the [highest trade union membership in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_union#Prevalence_worldwide "Trade union").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-ILO_Density-21) It maintains a [Nordic social welfare system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_model "Nordic model") that provides [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") and [tertiary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education "Tertiary education").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-22)[Iceland ranks highly in international comparisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_rankings_of_Iceland "International rankings of Iceland") of national performance, such as quality of life, education, protection of civil liberties, government transparency, and economic freedom. It has the smallest population of any [NATO member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_member "NATO member") and is the only one with [no standing army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_without_armed_forces "List of sovereign states without armed forces"), possessing only a lightly armed [coast guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Coast_Guard "Icelandic Coast Guard").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-23)

## Etymology

See also: [Names of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Iceland "Names of Iceland")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg/250px-Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Norsemen_Landing_in_Iceland.jpg)

Norsemen landing in Iceland – a 19th-century depiction by [Oscar Wergeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wergeland "Oscar Wergeland")

The _Landnámabók_ names [Naddodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naddodd "Naddodd") ([Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): _Naddoðr_) as the first [Norseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norseman "Norseman") to reach Iceland in the ninth century, having gotten lost while sailing from Norway to the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands"). He gave the island its first name of _Snæland_ (English: _Snowland_). The second explorer to arrive was the Swedish [Garðar Svavarsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gar%C3%B0ar_Svavarsson "Garðar Svavarsson"), who circumnavigated the island and named it _Garðarshólmur_ (English: _Garðar's Isle_) after himself.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-24)

The island's present name originated from [Flóki Vilgerðarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fl%C3%B3ki_Vilger%C3%B0arson "Flóki Vilgerðarson"), the first Norseman to intentionally travel to Iceland. According to the [Sagas of Icelanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagas_of_Icelanders "Sagas of Icelanders"), Flóki coined the name after he climbed a mountain, despondent after a harsh winter in present-day [Vatnsfjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatnsfj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Vatnsfjörður"), and saw an [ice cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_cap "Ice cap").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Evans-25) The notion that Iceland's settlers chose that name to discourage competing settlements is most likely a myth.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-Evans-25)

## History

Main article: [History of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland "History of Iceland")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Icelandic history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Icelandic_history "Timeline of Icelandic history").

### 874–1262: settlement and Commonwealth

See also: [Settlement of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_Iceland "Settlement of Iceland"), [Icelandic Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth"), and [Christianisation of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianisation_of_Iceland "Christianisation of Iceland")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Ingolf_by_Raadsig.jpg/250px-Ingolf_by_Raadsig.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ingolf_by_Raadsig.jpg)

[Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") (modern Icelandic: _Ingólfur Arnarson_), the first permanent Scandinavian settler

According to both _[Landnámabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landn%C3%A1mab%C3%B3k "Landnámabók")_ and _[Íslendingabók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Dslendingab%C3%B3k "Íslendingabók")_, monks known as the [Papar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papar "Papar") lived in Iceland before Scandinavian settlers arrived, possibly members of a [Hiberno-Scottish mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiberno-Scottish_mission "Hiberno-Scottish mission"). An archaeological excavation has revealed the ruins of a cabin in [Hafnir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafnir "Hafnir") on the [Reykjanes peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjanes_peninsula "Reykjanes peninsula"). [Carbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dating "Carbon dating") indicates that it was abandoned sometime between 770 and 880.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-26) In 2016, archaeologists uncovered a [longhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longhouse "Longhouse") in [Stöðvarfjörður](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%B6%C3%B0varfj%C3%B6r%C3%B0ur "Stöðvarfjörður") that may date to as early as 800.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-27)

Swedish Viking explorer [Garðar Svavarsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gar%C3%B0ar_Svavarsson "Garðar Svavarsson") was the first to circumnavigate Iceland in 870, and established that it was an island.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-28) He stayed during the winter and built a house in [Húsavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%BAsav%C3%ADk "Húsavík"). Garðar departed the following summer, but one of his men, [Náttfari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A1ttfari "Náttfari"), decided to stay behind with two slaves. Náttfari settled in what is now known as Náttfaravík, and he and his slaves became the first documented permanent residents of Iceland.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-30)

The Norwegian-Norse chieftain [Ingólfr Arnarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%B3lfr_Arnarson "Ingólfr Arnarson") built his homestead in present-day [Reykjavík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk "Reykjavík") in 874. Ingólfr was followed by many other emigrant settlers, largely Scandinavians and their [thralls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrall "Thrall"), many of whom were [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people") or [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-31) By 930, most [arable land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arable_land "Arable land") on the island had been claimed; the [Althing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althing "Althing"), a legislative and judicial assembly, was initiated to regulate the [Icelandic Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth"). The lack of arable land also served as an impetus to the [settlement of Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_settlements_in_Greenland "Norse settlements in Greenland") starting in 986.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-32) The period of these early settlements coincided with the [Medieval Warm Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Warm_Period "Medieval Warm Period"), when temperatures were similar to those of the early 20th century.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-33) At that time, about 25% of Iceland was covered with forest, compared to 1% in the present day.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-34)[Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") was adopted [by consensus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianisation_of_Iceland "Christianisation of Iceland") around 999–1000, although [Norse paganism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_paganism "Norse paganism") persisted among segments of the population for some years afterward.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-35)

### Iceland as a possession

#### Middle Ages

See also: [Age of the Sturlungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg/250px-Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grassodenh%C3%A4user.jpg)

[Turf houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_turf_house "Icelandic turf house") have been constructed since Iceland was settled in the 9th century.

The [Icelandic Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Commonwealth "Icelandic Commonwealth"), established in the 10th century, faced internal strife during the [Age of the Sturlungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Sturlungs "Age of the Sturlungs") (c. 1220–1264). This period was marked by violent conflicts among chieftains, notably the Sturlung family, leading to the weakening of the Commonwealth's political structure.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-36) The culmination of the struggles was the signing of the Old Covenant ([Gamli sáttmáli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamli_s%C3%A1ttm%C3%A1li "Gamli sáttmáli")) in 1262–1264, bringing [Iceland under Norwegian rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland "History of Iceland").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-37)

Environmental challenges further impacted [medieval Icelandic society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland "History of Iceland").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-38) Upon settlement, approximately 25–40% of Iceland was forested. However, extensive deforestation occurred as forests were cleared for timber, firewood, and to create grazing land for livestock. This led to significant soil erosion and a decline in arable land, exacerbating the difficulties of sustaining agriculture in Iceland's harsh climate.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-39) Agriculture during this period was predominantly pastoral, focusing on livestock such as sheep, cattle, and horses. While early settlers cultivated barley, the cooling climate from the 12th century onwards made grain cultivation increasingly difficult. The [Little Ice Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age "Little Ice Age") began around 1300, bringing colder and more unpredictable weather, further shortening growing seasons and making farming more challenging.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-40)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-41)

The [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") reached Iceland in 1402–1404 and again in 1494–1495, with devastating effects.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-42) The first outbreak is estimated to have killed 50–60% of the population, while the second resulted in a 30–50% mortality rate. These pandemics significantly reduced the population, leading to social and economic disruptions.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-43)

In 1380, after the death of [Haakon VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haakon_VI "Haakon VI"), his son [Olaf II of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olaf_II_of_Denmark "Olaf II of Denmark") succeeded to the Norwegian throne, uniting the crowns of Denmark and Norway under one monarch. Because Iceland was part of the Norwegian realm, it thereby came under the Danish-Norwegian crown. In 1397, the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") brought Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-45)

#### Reformation and the Early Modern period

See also: [Icelandic Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Reformation "Icelandic Reformation"), [Danish trade monopoly in Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_trade_monopoly_in_Iceland "Danish trade monopoly in Iceland"), and [Móðuharðindin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B3%C3%B0uhar%C3%B0indin "Móðuharðindin")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Bolungarvik_02.jpg/250px-Bolungarvik_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bolungarvik_02.jpg)

_Ósvör_, a replica of an old fishing outpost outside [Bolungarvík](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolungarv%C3%ADk "Bolungarvík")

Around the middle of the 16th century, as part of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation"), King [Christian III of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_III_of_Denmark "Christian III of Denmark") began to impose [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") on all his subjects. [Jón Arason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3n_Arason "Jón Arason"), the last Icelandic Catholic bishop, and two of his sons were beheaded in 1550. Iceland then became officially Lutheran, and Lutheranism has since remained the dominant religion.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas%2C_sive%2C_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_%2824696368309%29.jpg/250px-Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas%2C_sive%2C_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_%2824696368309%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerardi_Mercatoris_Atlas,_sive,_Cosmographicae_Meditationes_de_Fabrica_Mundi_et_Fabricati_Figura_(24696368309).jpg)

A map of Iceland published in the early 17th century by [Gerardus Mercator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerardus_Mercator "Gerardus Mercator")

In the 17th and 18th centuries, Denmark imposed [harsh trade restrictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Trade_Monopoly "Danish–Icelandic Trade Monopoly") on Iceland. Natural disasters, including volcanic eruptions and disease, contributed to a decreasing population. In the summer of 1627, [Barbary Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_Pirates "Barbary Pirates") committed the events known locally as the [Turkish Abductions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Abductions "Turkish Abductions"), in which hundreds of residents were taken into slavery in North Africa and dozens killed; this was the only invasion in Icelandic history to have caused casualties.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-46)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-47) The [1707–08 Iceland smallpox epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1707%E2%80%9308_Iceland_smallpox_epidemic "1707–08 Iceland smallpox epidemic") is estimated to have killed a quarter to a third of the population.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-48)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-49) In 1783 the [Laki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki "Laki") volcano erupted, with devastating effects.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-50) In the years following the eruption, known as the [Mist Hardships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mist_Hardships "Mist Hardships") ([Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language"): _Móðuharðindin_), over half of all livestock in the country died. Around a quarter of the population starved to death in the ensuing [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-51)

#### 1814–1918: independence movement

See also: [Icelandic independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_independence_movement "Icelandic independence movement") and [Fjölnir (journal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fj%C3%B6lnir_(journal) "Fjölnir (journal)")

After the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars") in 1814, Denmark-Norway broke up into two separate kingdoms under the [Treaty of Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Kiel "Treaty of Kiel"), but Iceland remained a Danish dependency. Throughout the 19th century, the country's climate continued to grow colder, resulting in mass emigration to the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World"), particularly to the region of [Gimli, Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimli,_Manitoba "Gimli, Manitoba") in Canada, which was sometimes referred to as [New Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Iceland "New Iceland"). About 15,000 people emigrated out of a total population of 70,000.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-52)

A national consciousness arose in the first half of the 19th century, inspired by [romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") and [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist "Nationalist") ideas from mainland Europe. An Icelandic independence movement took shape in the 1850s under the leadership of [Jón Sigurðsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3n_Sigur%C3%B0sson "Jón Sigurðsson"), based on the burgeoning Icelandic nationalism inspired by the _[Fjölnismenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fj%C3%B6lnismenn "Fjölnismenn")_ and other Danish-educated Icelandic intellectuals. In 1874, poet and clergyman [Matthías Jochumsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matth%C3%ADas_Jochumsson "Matthías Jochumsson") wrote the lyrics of "[Lofsöngur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lofs%C3%B6ngur "Lofsöngur")", which became the Icelandic [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem "National anthem"). Composer [Sveinbjörn Sveinbjörnsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveinbj%C3%B6rn_Sveinbj%C3%B6rnsson "Sveinbjörn Sveinbjörnsson") wrote the music.

In 1874, Denmark granted Iceland a constitution and limited home rule. That was expanded in 1904, and [Hannes Hafstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Hafstein "Hannes Hafstein") served as the first [Minister for Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Iceland "Minister for Iceland") in the Danish cabinet.

### 1918–1944: independence and the Kingdom of Iceland

See also: [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"), [Invasion of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Iceland "Invasion of Iceland"), and [Iceland in World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_in_World_War_II "Iceland in World War II")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/HMS_Berwick_%2865%29.jpg/250px-HMS_Berwick_%2865%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HMS_Berwick_(65).jpg)

[HMS _Berwick_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Berwick_(65) "HMS Berwick (65)") led the British [invasion of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Iceland "Invasion of Iceland").

The [Danish–Icelandic Act of Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish%E2%80%93Icelandic_Act_of_Union "Danish–Icelandic Act of Union"), an agreement with Denmark signed on 1 December 1918 and valid for 25 years, recognised Iceland as a fully sovereign and independent state in a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") with Denmark. The Government of Iceland established an embassy in Copenhagen and requested that Denmark carry out on its behalf certain defence and foreign affairs matters, subject to consultation with the Althing. Danish embassies around the world displayed two coats of arms and two flags: those of the Kingdom of Denmark and those of the [Kingdom of Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Iceland "Kingdom of Iceland"). Iceland's legal position became comparable to those of countries belonging to the Commonwealth of Nations, such as Canada, whose sovereign is King [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III").

During World War II, Iceland joined Denmark in asserting neutrality. After the [German occupation of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_occupation_of_Denmark "German occupation of Denmark") on 9 April 1940, the Althing replaced the king with a regent and declared that the Icelandic government would take control of its own defence and foreign affairs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-:0-53) A month later, British armed forces conducted [Operation Fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Fork "Operation Fork"), the invasion and occupation of the country, violating Icelandic [neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrality_(international_relations) "Neutrality (international relations)").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-54) In 1941, the Government of Iceland, friendly to Britain, invited the United States, then neutral, to take over its defence so that Britain could use its troops elsewhere.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland#cite_note-:0-53)
