### 1900s–onward (modern period)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1900s–onward (modern period)")]

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_%28cropped%2C_rotated_90%C2%B0%29.tif/lossy-page1-330px-Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_%28cropped%2C_rotated_90%C2%B0%29.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_(cropped,_rotated_90%C2%B0).tif)

Chromatic nyckelharpa by [August Bohlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bohlin "August Bohlin") (1877–1949)

The popularization of the nyckelharpa continued and by the early 20th century it had become an archetypal instrument for Swedish folk music, equivalent to the violin. From this point the instrument would see a wide range of developments to make it a more modern instrument for a modern audience.

[![Image 50](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_(cropped).tif)

[Eric Sahlström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sahlstr%C3%B6m "Eric Sahlström") (1912–1986) in 1967, playing nyckelharpa

Changes by [August Bohlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bohlin "August Bohlin") (1877–1949) in 1929/1930 made the nyckelharpa a [chromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic_scale "Chromatic scale") instrument with a straight [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(music) "Bow (music)"), making it a more violin-like and no longer a [bourdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") instrument.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9) Composer, player and maker of nyckelharpor [Eric Sahlström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sahlstr%C3%B6m "Eric Sahlström") (1912–1986) used this new instrument and helped to re-popularize it in the mid-20th century.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9) In spite of this, the nyckelharpa's popularity declined until the 1960s [roots revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_revival "Roots revival").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The 1960s and 1970s saw a resurgence in the popularity of the nyckelharpa, with notable artists such as [Marco Ambrosini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Ambrosini "Marco Ambrosini") (Italy and Germany), Sture Sahlström, Gille, Peter Puma Hedlund and Nils Nordström including the nyckelharpa in both [early music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_music "Early music") and [contemporary music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_music "Contemporary music") offerings. Continued refinement of the instrument also contributed to the increase in popularity, with instrument builders like [Jean-Claude Condi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Condi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jean-Claude Condi (page does not exist)") and [Annette Osann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Osann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Annette Osann (page does not exist)") bringing innovation to the bow and body.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-14)

In 1990s, the nyckelharpa was recognised as one of the instruments available for study at the folk music department of the [Royal College of Music in Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Music,_Stockholm "Royal College of Music, Stockholm") (_Kungliga Musikhögskolan_). It has also been a prominent part of several revival groups in the later part of the century, including the trio [Väsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4sen "Väsen"), the more contemporary group [Hedningarna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedningarna "Hedningarna"), the Finnish folk music group [Hyperborea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperborea_(Finnish_folk_music_group) "Hyperborea (Finnish folk music group)") and the Swedish folk music groups Dråm and [Nordman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordman "Nordman"). It has also been used in non-Scandinavian musical contexts, for example by the Spanish player [Ana Alcaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ana_Alcaide "Ana Alcaide"), the English singer and multi-instrumentalist [Anna Tam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Tam?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Tam (page does not exist)"), and Sandra Schmitt of Storm Seeker, a [pirate metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_metal "Pirate metal") band from Germany.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[Eurovision Song Contest 1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_1995 "Eurovision Song Contest 1995") winner Norway's song "Nocturne" (Secret Garden Group) used this instrument in their performance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-15)

The first World Nyckelharpa Day[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-auto-16) took place on 26 April 2020, just as the world had gone into lockdown for the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). All the events took place online, either as [livestreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_streaming "Live streaming") or pre-recorded videos on [Youtube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"). This is now a yearly event taking place on the Sunday closest to 26 April – this being the birthday of the great nyckelharpa player [Byss-Calle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byss-Calle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Byss-Calle (page does not exist)"). The event is coordinated by British/Swedish nyckelharpa player Vicki Swan.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-18)

English composer [Natalie Holt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Holt "Natalie Holt") used nyckelharpa for background score of the [Disney+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") series _[Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki\_(TV\_series) "Loki (TV series)")_ from 2021.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-19)

## Reconstructional archaeology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reconstructional archaeology")]

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/Emilio_Villalba.-_Viola_de_teclas_medieval_%28Nickelharpa%29._Saltarello.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

_Siena-Harpa_ being played by musician Emilio Villalba

In the 21st century there has been a growing interest among enthusiasts to resurrect the early historical nyckelharpa designs. This has led to countless recreations of preserved historical copies, such as the [moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa") and esseharpa,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Soittimet-20) among others, but also a push to recreate nyckelharpa-designs only found in historical paintings, such as the one depicted in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy. Such projects can be seen as [reconstructional archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructional_archaeology "Reconstructional archaeology"), although reproductions are not always 1–1 clones of what is depicted in the old paintings.

The nyckelharpa depicted in Siena, Italy, has been dubbed _viola a chiavi di Siena_ (Italian for "Sienan keyed viola"), or simply _Siena-Harpa_ (also styled _Sienaharpa_, "Siena harp") for short, analog to the Swedish naming-theme, and such a reconstruction was produced as part of an international research project around 2020, built by professional [luthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luthier "Luthier") Alexander Pilz, a seasoned maker of nyckelharpor working out of [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig"), Germany.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Siena-Harpa-5) The popularisation of the Italian design has led other luthiers in recent years to produce reproductions of the depiction as well.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fiddle_klawiszowe-21)

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Technique")]

[![Image 51](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Vaxholm_8556_%281158877619%29.jpg/250px-Vaxholm_8556_%281158877619%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vaxholm_8556_(1158877619).jpg)

Traditional method of playing

The nyckelharpa is usually played with a strap around the neck, stabilised by the right arm. [Didier François](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Fran%C3%A7ois "Didier François"), a violinist and nyckelharpist from Belgium, is noted for using an unusual playing posture, holding the nyckelharpa vertically in front of the chest. This allows a wider range of motion for both arms. It also affects the tone and sound of the instrument.

Some players may use a violin bracket to keep the nyckelharpa away from the body so that it can swing freely, causing it to sound more "open" as its resonance is not damped.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Each nyckelharpa string is either a melody string, drone, or (in some instruments) resonance string. Melody strings are stopped using the keys, so different notes can be played when the string is bowed, depending on which key is depressed. Each key specifically stops one melody string. Drone strings are bowed but not stopped, so only one note can be played with them. Resonance strings are neither bowed nor stopped. They add to the [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre") of the instrument by resonating in sympathy when the same note is played by bowing another string.

## Variants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Variants")]

![Image 52](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1d/Information_icon4.svg/20px-Information_icon4.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This list is [incomplete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Incomplete_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists"); you can help by [adding missing items](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit). _(June 2026)_

There are several variants of the nyckelharpa being produced and played today, differing in the number and arrangement of keys, number and arrangement of strings, and general body shape. They can be divided into types "with resonance strings" and types "without resonance strings".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_1990-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.org_history-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-olov_johansson-25) There are also a variety of derivatives which belongs to the "keyed [bowed chordophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowed_string_instrument "Bowed string instrument")-family" but do not necessarily have to be classified as nyckelharpor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Viola_d'amore_a_chiavi-6)

Listed types below refer to Swedish/Nordic types as "variants", with other types being referred to as "derivatives".

### Variants with resonance strings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Variants with resonance strings")]

The most common types of nyckelharpor are distinguished by having resonance strings. They can be divided into several subvariants, but the four main variants are as follows:[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.org_history-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-olov_johansson-25)

*   **Kromatisk nyckelharpa** ("[chromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic "Chromatic") key harp") – most predominant type of nyckelharpa. The three-row so-called "chromatic nyckelharpa", with three melody strings tuned A1 – C1 – G, one drone tuned at C (from the highest to the lowest string) that is only touched occasionally, and 12 resonance strings (one for each step of the chromatic scale).
*   **Kontrabasharpa** ("double bass harp") – most popular during the 17th and 18th centuries. Typically the top has a high arch, and there are two oval-shaped soundholes in the lower bout called _oxögon_. The name "Kontrabasharpa" refers not to the pitch being any deeper than a standard nyckelharpa's (it isn't), but to the unstopped [drone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_string "Drone string") which always resonates below the melody strings during regular play. The two melody strings are set up on either side of the drone string, such that melodies can be played as double stops between a single melody string and the open drone string without the two melody strings ever clashing.
*   **Silverbasharpa** ("silver bass harp") – most popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries, so named because of the bass strings which are traditionally wound with silver. It is the immediate predecessor to the modern nyckelharpa, and the string configuration is identical, however it retains the older top with a more pronounced arch as well as the two _oxögon_. The main difference is that only the top two strings are stopped, meaning that the bottom C and G strings cannot play any other notes, and so nearly all of its repertoire is in the key of C. In addition, some silverbasharpor may be diatonic and not chromatic, and some keys may stop both melody strings at once.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-26)
*   **Oktavharpa** ("octave harp") – invented by Lennart and Johan Hedin in 1996. It is essentially a modern three-row nyckelharpa tuned an octave down, almost identical to a cello. It is the lowest-pitched variant of the nyckelharpa.

The resonance strings, or [sympathetic strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_strings "Sympathetic strings"), which were added to the instrument during the 2nd half of the 16th century, are not bowed directly but resonate with the other strings. There can be anywhere from six to twelve of them, depending on the construction and tonality of the instrument. Some modern nyckelharpor have been made with four or even five rows of keys, however they have not been popular enough to replace the three-row nyckelharpa as the standard.

### Variants without resonance strings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Variants without resonance strings")]

Beyond the common variants with resonance strings, there are a variety of nyckelharpa designs without such. Some of examples include:

[![Image 53](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Moraharpa.jpg/250px-Moraharpa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moraharpa.jpg)

[Moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa") dated 1526 in the [Zorn Collections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zorn_Collections "Zorn Collections"), [Mora Municipality, Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mora_Municipality,_Sweden "Mora Municipality, Sweden")

*   **[Moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa")** ("Mora harp") – is the most common nyckelharpa derivative, based on a unique nyckelharpa found in the Swedish town of [Mora Municipality, Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mora_Municipality,_Sweden "Mora Municipality, Sweden"), dating to 1526 (although presumed to be from the later 17th century). This design has a straight bridge, one melody string, two drone strings, and one row of keys, with a body resembling a [lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute "Lute").
*   **Esseharpa** ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language") for "Esse harp") or **ähtävän harppu** ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language") for "Ähtävä harp") – Finnish/[Fenno-Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenno-Swedish "Fenno-Swedish") nyckelharpa derivative, based on nyckelharpa examples from Fenno-Swedish former municipality [Esse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esse,_Finland "Esse, Finland") ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"): _Ähtävä_) in the Finnish region of [Ostrobothnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrobothnia_(administrative_region) "Ostrobothnia (administrative region)") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Österbotten_). It is small and cone-shaped with four (sometimes three) strings and one row of ten to fifteen keys.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Soittimet-20)
*   **Vefsenharpa** ("Vefsn harp") – Norwegian nyckelharpa derivative, based on nyckelharpa examples from [Vefsn Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vefsn_Municipality "Vefsn Municipality") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Vefsen_) in [Nordland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordland "Nordland") county, [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"). Similar to the Esseharpa but with inward curves on the body.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)

### Derivatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Derivatives")]

*   **Viola a chiavi di Siena** ("Sienan keyed viola") or **Siena-Harpa** ("Siena harp") for short – is a nyckelharpa derivative based on the previously mentioned 1408 fresco by [Taddeo di Bartolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taddeo_di_Bartolo "Taddeo di Bartolo") at the [Palazzo Pubblico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Pubblico "Palazzo Pubblico") chapel in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy, featuring an angel playing a nyckelharpa. As part of [reconstructional archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructional_archaeology "Reconstructional archaeology"), this recreated design has three melody strings, one drone string, and one row of keys.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Siena-Harpa-5)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fiddle_klawiszowe-21)
*   **Viola d'amore a chiavi** ("keyed [viola d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_d'amore "Viola d'amore")") – is a nyckelharpa derivative seemingly invented by professional [luthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luthier "Luthier") Alexander Pilz, a seasoned maker of nyckelharpor from [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig"), Germany. It has gut strings and is specially built for [renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music")-[baroque music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_music "Baroque music"). It has a different sound than traditional Swedish Nyckelharpor, closer to the [viola da gamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_da_gamba "Viola da gamba"), and therefore has the name "keyed [viola d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_d'amore "Viola d'amore")".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Viola_d'amore_a_chiavi-6)

_**Nyckelharpa**_ (Swedish:[[ˈnʏ̂kːɛlˌharːpa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish"), roughly "keyed fiddle" in [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"), lit.'key-harp', plural: _nyckelharpor_) is a "keyed" [bowed chordophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowed_string_instrument "Bowed string instrument"), primarily originating from Sweden in its modern form, but with its historical roots scattered across medieval Europe. It is similar in appearance to a [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle") or [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_family "Violin family") but larger (in its earlier forms essentially a modified [vielle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vielle "Vielle")), which employs key-actuated tangents along the neck to change the pitch during play, much like a [hurdy-gurdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy "Hurdy-gurdy"). The keys slide under the strings, with the tangents set perpendicularly to the keys, reaching above the strings. Upon key-actuation, the tangent is pressed to meet the corresponding string, much like a [fret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fret "Fret"), shortening its vibrating length to that point, changing the pitch of the string.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.org/about-2) It is primarily played underarm, suspended from the shoulder using a [sling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sling_(firearms) "Sling (firearms)"), with the bow in the overhanging arm.

The origin of the instrument is unknown, but its historical foothold and modern development is much larger in Sweden than other countries, that being the only country with an unbroken usage. Many of the early historical depictions of the instrument are found in Sweden, with the earliest probable depiction being found on a relief located on a 14th century church portal. While historically, relatively speaking, not too common an instrument in Sweden, the violin outshining it in usage among [spelmän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spelman_(music) "Spelman (music)") (players of [Swedish folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_folk_music "Swedish folk music")), the nyckelharpa became a popular [folk instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_instrument "Folk instrument") in the Swedish province of [Uppland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland "Uppland") during the 17th century, subsequently leading to its popularization and spread throughout Sweden the following centuries. By the 19th century it had become a "fine" instrument, being played at concerts in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Motion_2001/02:Kr353-3) and by the early 20th century it had become an archetypal instrument alongside the violin for Swedish folk music. Today it is considered by many to be the quintessential national instrument of Sweden.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-4) The oldest surviving nyckelharpa is dated 1526 and is part of the [Zorn Collections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zorn_Collections "Zorn Collections") in [Mora Municipality, Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mora_Municipality,_Sweden "Mora Municipality, Sweden").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Motion_2001/02:Kr353-3)

Besides Sweden, early depictions of nyckelharpor can also be found in Denmark, Germany and Italy, among other European countries. The earliest of these is found in a 1408 [fresco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresco "Fresco") by [Taddeo di Bartolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taddeo_di_Bartolo "Taddeo di Bartolo") at the [Palazzo Pubblico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Pubblico "Palazzo Pubblico") chapel in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy, which depicts an angel playing a "keyed viola". Recently there has been a push by [luthiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luthier "Luthier") and the like to make recreations of these older depictions of nyckelharpor, akin to [reconstructional archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructional_archaeology "Reconstructional archaeology"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Siena-Harpa-5) but also new instruments based on the nyckelharpa concept of a keyed bow instrument.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Viola_d'amore_a_chiavi-6)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

_Nyckelharpa_ is the Swedish name for the instrument, composed of the lead _nyckel_ ("key"), and the follower _harpa_ ("harp"). Key is another word for tangent, while harp is an archaic word for string instrument, like a [lyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyre "Lyre"); see [Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): _harpa_, [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_language "Old English language"): _hearpe_, essentially "plucked string instrument". Compare _[tagelharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagelharpa "Tagelharpa")_ ("horsehair-harp"), another Nordic instrument, or even [jaw harp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaw_harp "Jaw harp"), where harp just means instrument.

Synonymes include _knaverharpa_, the same compound, but with the lead _knaver_, which means tangent in this sense, and is cognate to English "knob" (compare "doorkey" in the sense of doorknob). Another form is _nyckelgiga_, "key-fiddle"; _giga_ stemming from [Middle Low German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Low_German_language "Middle Low German language"): _gige_ ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): _Geige_), meaning fiddle.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-NE_giga-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### 1000s–1200s (first keyed instruments)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1000s–1200s (first keyed instruments)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Organistrumsantiago20060414_%28cropped_2%29.jpg/250px-Organistrumsantiago20060414_%28cropped_2%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Organistrumsantiago20060414_(cropped_2).jpg)

Stone relief of an [organistrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organistrum "Organistrum"), one of the first keyed string instruments

Development of keyed string instruments appears to have started during the [High Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Middle_Ages "High Middle Ages"), with instruments such as the duo-played [organistrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organistrum "Organistrum") (a [hurdy-gurdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy "Hurdy-gurdy")), starting in the late 900s or early 1000s. Such were popular in Southwestern Europe and eventually evolved into the solo-played "[symphonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonia "Symphonia")"-hurdy-gurdy in France or Spain in the 1200s, featuring [diatonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatonic "Diatonic") tangents. Somewhere along the line, it appears the keyboard of a "hurdy-gurdy" was integrated onto a [bowed string instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowed_string_instrument "Bowed string instrument"), producing the first keyed fiddle or proto-nyckelharpa instrument. It is unclear where the instrument first appeared, but the spread of hurdy-gurdy and bowed string instruments in Europe during the later Middle Ages makes it possible that the instrument was invented independently by several people.

In the [Late Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages"), the first depictions of nyckelharpor, or rather "keyed [vielles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vielle "Vielle")" by appearance, appear. The earliest possible depiction known can be found in a relief on one of the portals to the [Källunge Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4llunge_Church "Källunge Church"), located on the Swedish island of [Gotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotland "Gotland"). Dating from circa 1350, it depicts two musicians with bow stringed instruments suspiciously looking like nyckelharpor, appearing to have keyboxes (a cover above the strings) like a hurdy-gurdy. The relief is however [eroded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eroded "Eroded") and damaged from time, making it hard to confirm them as nyckelharpor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9)

The earliest confirmed depiction of a nyckelharpa appears in an Italian church painting found in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy, dating to 1408. It depicts an angel playing a [vielle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vielle "Vielle")-looking nyckelharpa (a common nyckelharpa motif for the period), featuring five keyes and a keybox above the strings.

Throughout the 15th century, more depictions of nyckelharpor start appearing in church paintings, notably in Swedish and Danish churches, such as the [Emmislöv Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmisl%C3%B6v_Church "Emmislöv Church"), which has a painting of a nyckelharpa musician dating to 1450–1475,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-history_per-ulf-10) and [Lagga Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagga_Church "Lagga Church"), which is dated to 1498.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpsfolket-11) Others include the [Tolfta Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolfta_Church?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tolfta Church (page does not exist)") in Sweden, which has two paintings of angels playing nyckelharpa, dating to c.1460–1525. Interestingly, most Swedish nyckelharpa depictions on church paintings, lack keyboxes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-history_per-ulf-10) Early Danish nyckelharpa depictions, such as the ones found in the Rynkeby Church, dated to ca. 1560, all feature keyboxes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-history_per-ulf-10)

Nyckelharpa finds (hover for info) in Germany-Poland (16th–17th century)

The earliest known recorded name for nyckelharpor can be found in an early German music dictionary _Musica Instrumentalis Deudsch_ by [Martin Agricola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Agricola "Martin Agricola"), dating to 1529. There it is called a _Schlüsselfidel_ ("key vielle").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-history_per-ulf-10) The corresponding image features a keybox on the instrument.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-history_per-ulf-10) The term later appears in _Theatrum Instrumentorum_, a famous work written in 1619 by the German organist [Michael Praetorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Praetorius "Michael Praetorius") (1571–1621).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12) It was illustrated in 1620 and the corresponding image also feature a keybox, albeit shown in opened position flipped up to the side.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

It has been noted, that both authors originated from and lived their lives in a German-Polish border area, which is interesting, considering the circumstance that within this region, the local musical instrument tradition, distinctively features a number of instruments with the same special features and peculiarities as that of the later Uppland nyckelharpa.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12) To add to this, there is a wooden nyckelharpa depiction from [Hildesheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hildesheim "Hildesheim") in the same general area as discussed, originally from 1529, albeit destroyed on 22 March 1945 during a bombing raid as part of [WWII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWII "WWII"), later being refabricated from photographs in the 1980s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

Agricola and Prætorius are noted to also be the only period authors outside of Denmark and Sweden to mention the nyckelharpa, even if only briefly without elaborate information. Both authors wrote that the nyckelharpa belonged to the lowest social classes, with Prætorius even saying that their instrument should hardly be considered music and thus not worth mentioning.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12) The nyckelharpa being an instrument of the lower classes is supported by Danish period author [Peder Syv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peder_Syv "Peder Syv"), as he, in a language book from 1663, expresses that "certain poets are no more writers than bagpipers and "key fiddlers" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _nøglefedlere_) are real musicians. It should, however, be noted, that the term "key fiddle" (_nøglefeile_) is a bit ambiguous, as Danish author [Hans Mikkelsen Ravn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Mikkelsen_Ravn?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hans Mikkelsen Ravn (page does not exist)")[[da](https://da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans%20Mikkelsen%20Ravn "da:Hans Mikkelsen Ravn")], used the term in 1646 for a supposed "[hurdy-gurdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy "Hurdy-gurdy")".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

It can be assumed that nyckelharpor went out of style in Germany fairly early on. A German-born tobacco manufacturer in [Karlskrona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlskrona "Karlskrona"), Sweden, named _Stefanus Cyrillus Rettig_ (1750–1828), is recounted in a 1939 source, of how, in his youth in [Pomerania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomerania "Pomerania"), Germany, he saw old nyckelharpa instruments stored away on cupboards in rooms, but that they were so archaic that no one knew anything about them.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

Nyckelharpa finds in Finland (late 17th century)

There are written sources that indicate that nyckelharpor existed in the area around Swedish speaking [Närpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A4rpes "Närpes"), Finland, in the late 17th century and early 18th century, and even though the instruments are often referred to in literature as "_nyckijl pijga_", the correct term is probably nyckel "_nyckijl gijga_"[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fom.journal.fi-13) (modern Swedish: _nyckelgiga_, "key fiddle"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-NE_giga-7) which was a common name for nyckelharpa.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fom.journal.fi-13)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-NE_giga-7) This conforms with the [Esseharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esseharpa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Esseharpa (page does not exist)") from [Esse, Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esse,_Finland "Esse, Finland"), which is dated to the late 17th century.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fom.journal.fi-13)

### 1600s–1800s (early modern period)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1600s–1800s (early modern period)")]

At the turn of the 17th century, the nyckelharpa was not too common an instrument in Sweden, the violin outshining it in [Swedish folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_folk_music "Swedish folk music"); however, starting from the early 17th century, the nyckelharpa got a foothold as a popular [folk instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_instrument "Folk instrument") among [spelmän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spelman_(music) "Spelman (music)") (players of [Swedish folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_folk_music "Swedish folk music")) in the Swedish province of [Uppland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppland "Uppland"), which came to be the stronghold for nyckelharpa music the following centuries, including musicians like [Byss-Calle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byss-Calle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Byss-Calle (page does not exist)")[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byss-Calle "sv:Byss-Calle")] (Carl Ersson Bössa, 1783–1847) from [Älvkarleby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%84lvkarleby "Älvkarleby").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9) It can be found briefly in Swedish records from 1603 onwards, then primarily in court records and prose texts, however, occasional details are found in treatises from 1684, 1686, 1698, 1702 and 1717.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12) In the oldest material, scholars used the term _nyckelgiga_ ("key-_giga_", the latter also being a generic old word for instrument), eventually disappearing in favour of nyckelharpa and thereof.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

From Uppland, the popularisation of the instrument spread to the neighbouring provinces and eventually throughout Sweden. By the 19th century it had become a "fine" instrument which came to be played at concerts in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Motion_2001/02:Kr353-3) and in 1899 the first detailed description of the instrument was given.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.eu-12)

### 1900s–onward (modern period)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1900s–onward (modern period)")]

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_%28cropped%2C_rotated_90%C2%B0%29.tif/lossy-page1-330px-Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_%28cropped%2C_rotated_90%C2%B0%29.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kromatisk_nyckelharpa_-_SMV_-_X5662_01_01_01_(cropped,_rotated_90%C2%B0).tif)

Chromatic nyckelharpa by [August Bohlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bohlin "August Bohlin") (1877–1949)

The popularization of the nyckelharpa continued and by the early 20th century it had become an archetypal instrument for Swedish folk music, equivalent to the violin. From this point the instrument would see a wide range of developments to make it a more modern instrument for a modern audience.

[![Image 50](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ok%C3%A4nd_spelman_-_SMV_-_Jan_Lings_arkiv_Vol_3_080_(cropped).tif)

[Eric Sahlström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sahlstr%C3%B6m "Eric Sahlström") (1912–1986) in 1967, playing nyckelharpa

Changes by [August Bohlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bohlin "August Bohlin") (1877–1949) in 1929/1930 made the nyckelharpa a [chromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic_scale "Chromatic scale") instrument with a straight [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(music) "Bow (music)"), making it a more violin-like and no longer a [bourdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") instrument.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9) Composer, player and maker of nyckelharpor [Eric Sahlström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sahlstr%C3%B6m "Eric Sahlström") (1912–1986) used this new instrument and helped to re-popularize it in the mid-20th century.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-World-9) In spite of this, the nyckelharpa's popularity declined until the 1960s [roots revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roots_revival "Roots revival").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The 1960s and 1970s saw a resurgence in the popularity of the nyckelharpa, with notable artists such as [Marco Ambrosini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Ambrosini "Marco Ambrosini") (Italy and Germany), Sture Sahlström, Gille, Peter Puma Hedlund and Nils Nordström including the nyckelharpa in both [early music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_music "Early music") and [contemporary music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_music "Contemporary music") offerings. Continued refinement of the instrument also contributed to the increase in popularity, with instrument builders like [Jean-Claude Condi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Condi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jean-Claude Condi (page does not exist)") and [Annette Osann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Osann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Annette Osann (page does not exist)") bringing innovation to the bow and body.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-14)

In 1990s, the nyckelharpa was recognised as one of the instruments available for study at the folk music department of the [Royal College of Music in Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Music,_Stockholm "Royal College of Music, Stockholm") (_Kungliga Musikhögskolan_). It has also been a prominent part of several revival groups in the later part of the century, including the trio [Väsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4sen "Väsen"), the more contemporary group [Hedningarna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedningarna "Hedningarna"), the Finnish folk music group [Hyperborea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperborea_(Finnish_folk_music_group) "Hyperborea (Finnish folk music group)") and the Swedish folk music groups Dråm and [Nordman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordman "Nordman"). It has also been used in non-Scandinavian musical contexts, for example by the Spanish player [Ana Alcaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ana_Alcaide "Ana Alcaide"), the English singer and multi-instrumentalist [Anna Tam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Tam?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anna Tam (page does not exist)"), and Sandra Schmitt of Storm Seeker, a [pirate metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_metal "Pirate metal") band from Germany.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[Eurovision Song Contest 1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_1995 "Eurovision Song Contest 1995") winner Norway's song "Nocturne" (Secret Garden Group) used this instrument in their performance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-15)

The first World Nyckelharpa Day[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-auto-16) took place on 26 April 2020, just as the world had gone into lockdown for the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). All the events took place online, either as [livestreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_streaming "Live streaming") or pre-recorded videos on [Youtube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"). This is now a yearly event taking place on the Sunday closest to 26 April – this being the birthday of the great nyckelharpa player [Byss-Calle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byss-Calle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Byss-Calle (page does not exist)"). The event is coordinated by British/Swedish nyckelharpa player Vicki Swan.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-18)

English composer [Natalie Holt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Holt "Natalie Holt") used nyckelharpa for background score of the [Disney+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") series _[Loki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki\_(TV\_series) "Loki (TV series)")_ from 2021.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-19)

## Reconstructional archaeology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reconstructional archaeology")]

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/Emilio_Villalba.-_Viola_de_teclas_medieval_%28Nickelharpa%29._Saltarello.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

_Siena-Harpa_ being played by musician Emilio Villalba

In the 21st century there has been a growing interest among enthusiasts to resurrect the early historical nyckelharpa designs. This has led to countless recreations of preserved historical copies, such as the [moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa") and esseharpa,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Soittimet-20) among others, but also a push to recreate nyckelharpa-designs only found in historical paintings, such as the one depicted in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy. Such projects can be seen as [reconstructional archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructional_archaeology "Reconstructional archaeology"), although reproductions are not always 1–1 clones of what is depicted in the old paintings.

The nyckelharpa depicted in Siena, Italy, has been dubbed _viola a chiavi di Siena_ (Italian for "Sienan keyed viola"), or simply _Siena-Harpa_ (also styled _Sienaharpa_, "Siena harp") for short, analog to the Swedish naming-theme, and such a reconstruction was produced as part of an international research project around 2020, built by professional [luthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luthier "Luthier") Alexander Pilz, a seasoned maker of nyckelharpor working out of [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig"), Germany.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Siena-Harpa-5) The popularisation of the Italian design has led other luthiers in recent years to produce reproductions of the depiction as well.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fiddle_klawiszowe-21)

## Technique

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Technique")]

[![Image 51](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Vaxholm_8556_%281158877619%29.jpg/250px-Vaxholm_8556_%281158877619%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vaxholm_8556_(1158877619).jpg)

Traditional method of playing

The nyckelharpa is usually played with a strap around the neck, stabilised by the right arm. [Didier François](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Fran%C3%A7ois "Didier François"), a violinist and nyckelharpist from Belgium, is noted for using an unusual playing posture, holding the nyckelharpa vertically in front of the chest. This allows a wider range of motion for both arms. It also affects the tone and sound of the instrument.

Some players may use a violin bracket to keep the nyckelharpa away from the body so that it can swing freely, causing it to sound more "open" as its resonance is not damped.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Each nyckelharpa string is either a melody string, drone, or (in some instruments) resonance string. Melody strings are stopped using the keys, so different notes can be played when the string is bowed, depending on which key is depressed. Each key specifically stops one melody string. Drone strings are bowed but not stopped, so only one note can be played with them. Resonance strings are neither bowed nor stopped. They add to the [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre") of the instrument by resonating in sympathy when the same note is played by bowing another string.

## Variants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Variants")]

![Image 52](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1d/Information_icon4.svg/20px-Information_icon4.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This list is [incomplete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Incomplete_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists"); you can help by [adding missing items](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit). _(June 2026)_

There are several variants of the nyckelharpa being produced and played today, differing in the number and arrangement of keys, number and arrangement of strings, and general body shape. They can be divided into types "with resonance strings" and types "without resonance strings".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_1990-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.org_history-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-olov_johansson-25) There are also a variety of derivatives which belongs to the "keyed [bowed chordophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowed_string_instrument "Bowed string instrument")-family" but do not necessarily have to be classified as nyckelharpor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Viola_d'amore_a_chiavi-6)

Listed types below refer to Swedish/Nordic types as "variants", with other types being referred to as "derivatives".

### Variants with resonance strings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Variants with resonance strings")]

The most common types of nyckelharpor are distinguished by having resonance strings. They can be divided into several subvariants, but the four main variants are as follows:[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-nyckelharpa.org_history-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-olov_johansson-25)

*   **Kromatisk nyckelharpa** ("[chromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic "Chromatic") key harp") – most predominant type of nyckelharpa. The three-row so-called "chromatic nyckelharpa", with three melody strings tuned A1 – C1 – G, one drone tuned at C (from the highest to the lowest string) that is only touched occasionally, and 12 resonance strings (one for each step of the chromatic scale).
*   **Kontrabasharpa** ("double bass harp") – most popular during the 17th and 18th centuries. Typically the top has a high arch, and there are two oval-shaped soundholes in the lower bout called _oxögon_. The name "Kontrabasharpa" refers not to the pitch being any deeper than a standard nyckelharpa's (it isn't), but to the unstopped [drone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_string "Drone string") which always resonates below the melody strings during regular play. The two melody strings are set up on either side of the drone string, such that melodies can be played as double stops between a single melody string and the open drone string without the two melody strings ever clashing.
*   **Silverbasharpa** ("silver bass harp") – most popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries, so named because of the bass strings which are traditionally wound with silver. It is the immediate predecessor to the modern nyckelharpa, and the string configuration is identical, however it retains the older top with a more pronounced arch as well as the two _oxögon_. The main difference is that only the top two strings are stopped, meaning that the bottom C and G strings cannot play any other notes, and so nearly all of its repertoire is in the key of C. In addition, some silverbasharpor may be diatonic and not chromatic, and some keys may stop both melody strings at once.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-26)
*   **Oktavharpa** ("octave harp") – invented by Lennart and Johan Hedin in 1996. It is essentially a modern three-row nyckelharpa tuned an octave down, almost identical to a cello. It is the lowest-pitched variant of the nyckelharpa.

The resonance strings, or [sympathetic strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_strings "Sympathetic strings"), which were added to the instrument during the 2nd half of the 16th century, are not bowed directly but resonate with the other strings. There can be anywhere from six to twelve of them, depending on the construction and tonality of the instrument. Some modern nyckelharpor have been made with four or even five rows of keys, however they have not been popular enough to replace the three-row nyckelharpa as the standard.

### Variants without resonance strings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Variants without resonance strings")]

Beyond the common variants with resonance strings, there are a variety of nyckelharpa designs without such. Some of examples include:

[![Image 53](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Moraharpa.jpg/250px-Moraharpa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moraharpa.jpg)

[Moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa") dated 1526 in the [Zorn Collections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zorn_Collections "Zorn Collections"), [Mora Municipality, Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mora_Municipality,_Sweden "Mora Municipality, Sweden")

*   **[Moraharpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraharpa "Moraharpa")** ("Mora harp") – is the most common nyckelharpa derivative, based on a unique nyckelharpa found in the Swedish town of [Mora Municipality, Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mora_Municipality,_Sweden "Mora Municipality, Sweden"), dating to 1526 (although presumed to be from the later 17th century). This design has a straight bridge, one melody string, two drone strings, and one row of keys, with a body resembling a [lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute "Lute").
*   **Esseharpa** ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language") for "Esse harp") or **ähtävän harppu** ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language") for "Ähtävä harp") – Finnish/[Fenno-Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenno-Swedish "Fenno-Swedish") nyckelharpa derivative, based on nyckelharpa examples from Fenno-Swedish former municipality [Esse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esse,_Finland "Esse, Finland") ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"): _Ähtävä_) in the Finnish region of [Ostrobothnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrobothnia_(administrative_region) "Ostrobothnia (administrative region)") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Österbotten_). It is small and cone-shaped with four (sometimes three) strings and one row of ten to fifteen keys.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Soittimet-20)
*   **Vefsenharpa** ("Vefsn harp") – Norwegian nyckelharpa derivative, based on nyckelharpa examples from [Vefsn Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vefsn_Municipality "Vefsn Municipality") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Vefsen_) in [Nordland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordland "Nordland") county, [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"). Similar to the Esseharpa but with inward curves on the body.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-typo_short-22)

### Derivatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nyckelharpa&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Derivatives")]

*   **Viola a chiavi di Siena** ("Sienan keyed viola") or **Siena-Harpa** ("Siena harp") for short – is a nyckelharpa derivative based on the previously mentioned 1408 fresco by [Taddeo di Bartolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taddeo_di_Bartolo "Taddeo di Bartolo") at the [Palazzo Pubblico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Pubblico "Palazzo Pubblico") chapel in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy, featuring an angel playing a nyckelharpa. As part of [reconstructional archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructional_archaeology "Reconstructional archaeology"), this recreated design has three melody strings, one drone string, and one row of keys.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Siena-Harpa-5)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-fiddle_klawiszowe-21)
*   **Viola d'amore a chiavi** ("keyed [viola d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_d'amore "Viola d'amore")") – is a nyckelharpa derivative seemingly invented by professional [luthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luthier "Luthier") Alexander Pilz, a seasoned maker of nyckelharpor from [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig"), Germany. It has gut strings and is specially built for [renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music")-[baroque music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_music "Baroque music"). It has a different sound than traditional Swedish Nyckelharpor, closer to the [viola da gamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_da_gamba "Viola da gamba"), and therefore has the name "keyed [viola d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_d'amore "Viola d'amore")".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyckelharpa#cite_note-Viola_d'amore_a_chiavi-6)
