**Denmark**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-17) is a [Nordic country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_countries "Nordic countries") in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe"). It is the [metropole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropole "Metropole") and most populous constituent of the Kingdom of Denmark,[[N 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-18) also known as the [Danish Realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Realm "Danish Realm"), a [constitutionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution "Constitution")[unitary state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") that includes the [autonomous territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_administrative_division "Autonomous administrative division") of the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands") and [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland") in the north [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-territory-19) Metropolitan Denmark,[[N 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-proper-20) also called "continental Denmark" or "Denmark proper",[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-21) consists of the northern [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland")[peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsula "Peninsula") and an [archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archipelago "Archipelago") of 406 islands.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-islands-22) It is the southernmost of the [Scandinavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") countries, lying southwest of Sweden, south of Norway, and north of Germany, with which it shares [a short border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Germany_border "Denmark–Germany border"). Metropolitan Denmark is situated between the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") to the west and the [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea "Baltic Sea") to the east.[[N 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-23)

The Kingdom of Denmark, including the Faroe Islands and Greenland, has roughly [1,400 islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Denmark "List of islands of Denmark") greater than 100 square metres (1,100 sq ft) in area; 443 have been named and 78 are inhabited.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-24) Denmark's population is over 6 million (1 May 2025),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Pop.Denmark-12) of which roughly 40% live in [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand "Zealand"), (Sjælland) the largest and most populated island in Metropolitan Denmark; [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), (København) the capital and largest city of the Danish Realm, is situated on Zealand and Amager and Slotsholmen.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-25) Composed mostly of flat, [arable land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arable_land "Arable land"), Denmark is characterised by sandy coasts, low elevation, and a [temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate"). Denmark exercises [hegemonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemony "Hegemony") influence in the [Danish Realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Realm "Danish Realm"), [devolving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devolution "Devolution") powers to the other constituent entities to handle their internal affairs. [Home rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_rule "Home rule") was established in the Faroe Islands in 1948; [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland") achieved home rule in 1979 and [further autonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Greenlandic_self-government_referendum "2008 Greenlandic self-government referendum") in 2009.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-26)

The [unified Kingdom of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Denmark "History of Denmark") emerged in the eighth century AD as a [maritime power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_power "Maritime power") amid the struggle for [control of the Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominium_maris_baltici "Dominium maris baltici").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoneBainBoothParnell200831-4) In 1397, it formed the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") with Norway and Sweden. This union persisted until Sweden's [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") in 1523. The remaining Kingdom of [Denmark–Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Norway "Denmark–Norway") endured a [series of wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Wars "Northern Wars") in the 17th century that resulted in [territorial cessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cession "Cession") to Sweden. A surge of [nationalist movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Denmark#The_19th_century "History of Denmark") in the 19th century were defeated by the Danes in the [First Schleswig War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Schleswig_War "First Schleswig War") of 1848. The adoption of the [Constitution of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Denmark "Constitution of Denmark") on 5 June 1849 ended the [absolute monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy "Absolute monarchy"). In the [Second Schleswig War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Schleswig_War "Second Schleswig War"), Denmark lost [Schleswig-Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig-Holstein "Schleswig-Holstein"), which led to changes in Danish politics henceforth emphasising social cohesion in the diminished realm, as well as the clearing of the vast moors of Jutland for agriculture, new Christian movements split between [Indre Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indre_Mission "Indre Mission") and [Grundtvig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._F._S._Grundtvig "N. F. S. Grundtvig"), but generally a stronger self-perception among the people of belonging to a unified country and state. In 1920, [North Schleswig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Schleswig "North Schleswig") became Danish again.

Denmark began industrialising in the mid 19th century, becoming a major agricultural exporter. It introduced [social and labour market reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanslergade_Agreement "Kanslergade Agreement") in the early 20th century, forming the basis for the present [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state")[model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_model "Nordic model") and advanced [mixed economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_economy "Mixed economy"). [Denmark remained neutral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_during_World_War_I "Denmark during World War I") during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"); Danish neutrality was violated in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") by a rapid [German invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_Denmark_(1940) "German invasion of Denmark (1940)") in April 1940. During occupation, a [resistance movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_resistance_movement "Danish resistance movement") emerged in 1943, while Iceland declared independence in 1944; Denmark was [liberated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_in_World_War_II#Hardship_and_the_end_of_the_war "Denmark in World War II") after the end of the war in May 1945. In 1973, Denmark, together with [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Greenland_from_the_European_Communities "Withdrawal of Greenland from the European Communities") but not the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands"), became a member of what is now the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"); however, it negotiated [certain opt-outs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union "Opt-outs in the European Union"), such as retaining its own currency, the [krone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_krone "Danish krone").

Denmark is a [developed country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country") with an advanced [high-income economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_high-income_economy "World Bank high-income economy"), high [standard of living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_of_living "Standard of living"), and robust [social welfare policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_model "Nordic model"). Danish culture and society are broadly progressive egalitarian, and [socially liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_liberalism "Social liberalism"); Denmark was the first country to legally recognise [same-sex partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_Denmark "Same-sex marriage in Denmark"). It is a founding member of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO"), the [Nordic Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_Council "Nordic Council"), the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD"), the [OSCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe "Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe"), the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe"), and the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), and is part of the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area"). Denmark maintains close political, cultural, and linguistic ties with its Scandinavian neighbours.

## Etymology

Main article: [Etymology of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymology_of_Denmark "Etymology of Denmark")

The etymology of the name "Denmark", the relationship between "Danes" and "Denmark", and the emergence of Denmark as a unified kingdom are topics of continuous scholarly debate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-27)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-28) This is centred primarily on the morpheme _"Dan"_ and whether it refers to the [Dani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes_(tribe) "Danes (tribe)") or a historical person [Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_(king) "Dan (king)") and the exact meaning of the -_"mark"_ ending.

Most etymological dictionaries and handbooks derive "Dan" from a word meaning "flat land", related to German _Tenne_ "threshing floor", English _den_ "cave".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-et1-29) The element _mark_ is believed to mean [woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland "Woodland") or [borderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border "Border") (see [marches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_(territory) "March (territory)")), with probable references to the border forests in south [Schleswig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Schleswig "Duchy of Schleswig").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-30)

The first recorded use of the word _Danmark_ within Denmark itself is found on the two [Jelling stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelling_stones "Jelling stones"), which are [runestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runestone "Runestone") believed to have been erected by [Gorm the Old](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorm_the_Old "Gorm the Old"), considered to be Denmark's first king, (c.955) and [Harald Bluetooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bluetooth "Harald Bluetooth") (c.965). The larger of the two stones is popularly cited as the "baptismal certificate" (_dåbsattest_) of Denmark,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-31) though both use the word "Denmark", in the [accusative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accusative_case "Accusative case")ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚢᚱᚴ _tanmaurk_ ([danmɒrk]) on the large stone, and the [genitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genitive_case "Genitive case")ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴᛅᚱ "tanmarkar" (pronounced [danmarkaɽ]) on the small stone, while the [dative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dative_case "Dative case") form _tąnmarku_ (pronounced [danmarkʊ]) is found on the contemporaneous Skivum stone. The inhabitants of Denmark are there called _tani_ ([danɪ]), or "Danes", in the accusative.

## History

Main article: [History of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Denmark "History of Denmark")

See also: [History of the Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Faroe_Islands "History of the Faroe Islands") and [History of Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Greenland "History of Greenland")

### Prehistory

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Solvognen-00100.jpg/250px-Solvognen-00100.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Solvognen-00100.jpg)

The gilded side of the [Trundholm sun chariot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trundholm_sun_chariot "Trundholm sun chariot") dating from the Nordic Bronze Age

The earliest [archaeological finds in Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_Denmark "Archaeology of Denmark") date back to the [Eem interglacial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eemian "Eemian") from 130,000 to 110,000 [BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anno_Domini "Anno Domini").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichaelsen200219-32) Denmark has been inhabited since around 12,500 BC and [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture") has been evident since 3900 BC.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-foreign_ministry-33) The [Nordic Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_Bronze_Age "Nordic Bronze Age") (1800–600 BC) in Denmark was marked by [burial mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus"), which left an abundance of findings including [lurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lur "Lur") and the [Sun Chariot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trundholm_sun_chariot "Trundholm sun chariot").

During the [Pre-Roman Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Roman_Iron_Age "Pre-Roman Iron Age") (500 BC– AD 1), native groups began migrating south, and the first tribal [Danes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes_(tribe) "Danes (tribe)") came to the country between the Pre-Roman and the [Germanic Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_Iron_Age "Germanic Iron Age"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBusck200220-34) in the [Roman Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Iron_Age "Roman Iron Age") (AD 1–400).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-foreign_ministry-33) The [Roman provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_province "Roman province") maintained [trade routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") and relations with native tribes in Denmark, and [Roman coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_currency "Roman currency") have been found in Denmark. Evidence of strong [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_nations "Celtic nations") cultural influence dates from this period in Denmark and much of North-West Europe and is among other things reflected in the finding of the [Gundestrup cauldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gundestrup_cauldron "Gundestrup cauldron").

The tribal Danes came from the east [Danish islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Denmark "List of islands of Denmark") ([Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand "Zealand")) and [Scania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scania "Scania"), today Skåne in Southern Sweden, and spoke an early form of [North Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Germanic_languages "North Germanic languages"). Historians believe that before their arrival, most of [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland") and the nearest islands were settled by tribal [Jutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutes "Jutes"). Many Jutes migrated to [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain"), according to legend some as mercenaries of [Brythonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brythonic_languages "Brythonic languages") King [Vortigern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortigern "Vortigern"), and formed the south-eastern territories of [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), the [Isle of Wight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight "Isle of Wight") and other areas, where they settled. They were later absorbed or [ethnically cleansed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing "Ethnic cleansing") by the invading [Angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angles_(tribe) "Angles (tribe)") and [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons "Saxons"), who formed the [Anglo-Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons"). The remaining Jutish population in Jutland assimilated in with the settling [Danes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes_(tribe) "Danes (tribe)").

A short note about the _Dani_ in _[Getica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getica "Getica")_ by the historian [Jordanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordanes "Jordanes") is believed to be an early mention of the Danes, one of the [ethnic groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_group "Ethnic group") from whom modern [Danes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes "Danes") are descended.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBusck200219-35)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-36) The [Danevirke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danevirke "Danevirke") defence structures were built in phases from the 3rd century forward and the sheer size of the construction efforts in AD 737 are attributed to the emergence of a Danish king.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichaelsen2002122%E2%80%93123-37) A [new runic alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Younger_Futhark "Younger Futhark") was first used around the same time and [Ribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribe "Ribe"), the oldest town of Denmark, was founded about AD 700.

### Viking and Middle Ages

Main articles: [Viking Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age "Viking Age") and [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Ladbyskibet.jpg/250px-Ladbyskibet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ladbyskibet.jpg)

The [Ladby ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladby_ship "Ladby ship"), the largest ship burial found in Denmark

From the 8th to the 10th century the population of the wider [Scandinavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Scandinavia "History of Scandinavia") region was called [Vikings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikings "Vikings") by non-Scandinavians. While they mostly lived off agriculture, fishing and trade, they were excellent sailors and would travel as far as Iceland, Greenland and Canada. They traded in all parts of Europe, down to Constantinople and beyond, but would also raid local settlements and set up colonies in far-flung places. The Danish Vikings were most actively raiding the eastern and southern [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles") and [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"). They settled in parts of England (known as the [Danelaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danelaw "Danelaw")) under King [Sweyn Forkbeard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweyn_Forkbeard "Sweyn Forkbeard") in 1013, and in France where Danes and Norwegians were allowed to settle in what would become [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") in exchange of allegiance to [Robert I of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_I_of_France "Robert I of France") with [Rollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rollo "Rollo") as first ruler.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-38) Some [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons")[pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pence "Pence") of this period have been found in Denmark.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Lund-39)

Denmark was largely consolidated by the late 8th century and its rulers are consistently referred to in [Frankish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankish_language "Frankish language") sources as kings (_reges_). Under the reign of [Gudfred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudfred "Gudfred") in 804 the Danish kingdom may have included all the [lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lands_of_Denmark "Lands of Denmark") of Jutland, [Scania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scania "Scania") and the Danish islands, excluding Bornholm.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-40)

[![Image 18: Large stone containing a carved depiction of Jesus Christ](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Jellingsten_stor_1.jpg/250px-Jellingsten_stor_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jellingsten_stor_1.jpg)

Larger of the two Jelling stones, raised by [Harald Bluetooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bluetooth "Harald Bluetooth")

The extant Danish monarchy traces its roots back to [Gorm the Old](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorm_the_Old "Gorm the Old"), who established his reign in the early 10th century.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoneBainBoothParnell200831-4) As attested by the [Jelling stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelling_stones "Jelling stones"), the Danes were [Christianised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianised "Christianised") around 965 by [Harald Bluetooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bluetooth "Harald Bluetooth"), the son of Gorm and [Thyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyra "Thyra"). It is believed that Denmark became Christian for political reasons so as not to get invaded by the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"). A rising Christian power in Europe, the Holy Roman Empire was an important trading partner for the Danes. As a deterrent against this threat, Harald built six [fortresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortresses "Fortresses") around Denmark called [Trelleborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_ring_fortress "Viking ring fortress") and built a further [Danevirke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danevirke "Danevirke"). In the early 11th century, [Canute the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canute_the_Great "Canute the Great") won and united Denmark, England, and Norway for almost 30 years with a Scandinavian army.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Lund-39)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-41)

Throughout the [High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Middle_Ages "High Middle Ages") and [Late Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages"), Denmark also included [Skåneland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sk%C3%A5neland "Skåneland") (the areas of Scania, [Halland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halland "Halland"), and [Blekinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blekinge "Blekinge") in present-day southern Sweden) and Danish kings ruled [Danish Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Estonia "Danish Estonia"), as well as the [duchies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy "Duchy") of [Schleswig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig "Schleswig") and [Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holstein "Holstein"). Most of the latter two now form the state of [Schleswig-Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig-Holstein "Schleswig-Holstein") in northern Germany.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-42)

In 1397, Denmark entered into a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") known as the [Kalmar Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") with Norway and Sweden, united under Queen [Margaret I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_I_of_Denmark "Margaret I of Denmark").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoneBainBoothParnell200833-43)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-44)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-45) The three countries were to be treated as equals in the union. However, even from the start, Margaret may not have been so idealistic; treating Denmark as the clear "senior" partner of the union.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Lauring-46)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-47) Thus, much of the next 125 years of [Scandinavian history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Scandinavia "History of Scandinavia") revolves around this union, with Sweden breaking off and re-joining the Kalmar Union repeatedly. The issue was for practical purposes resolved on 17 June 1523, as [Swedish King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Swedish_monarchs "List of Swedish monarchs")[Gustav Vasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_I_of_Sweden "Gustav I of Sweden") conquered the city of [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"). The Protestant [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation") spread to Scandinavia in the 1530s, and following the [Count's Feud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count's_Feud "Count's Feud") civil war, [Denmark converted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation_in_Denmark%E2%80%93Norway_and_Holstein "Reformation in Denmark–Norway and Holstein") to [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") in 1536. Later that year, Denmark entered into a new union with Norway.

### Early modern history (1536–1849)

Main articles: [Denmark–Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Norway "Denmark–Norway") and [Danish overseas colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_overseas_colonies "Danish overseas colonies")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Denmark-Norway_in_1780.svg/250px-Denmark-Norway_in_1780.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Denmark-Norway_in_1780.svg)

Extent of the [Dano-Norwegian Realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Norway "Denmark–Norway"). After the Napoleonic Wars, Norway was ceded to Sweden while Denmark kept the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands"), [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), and Iceland.

After Sweden permanently [broke away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Sweden_(1523%E2%80%931611) "History of Sweden (1523–1611)") from the Kalmar Union, Denmark tried on several occasions to reassert control over its neighbour. King [Christian IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark") attacked Sweden in the 1611–1613 [Kalmar War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_War "Kalmar War") but failed to accomplish his main objective of forcing it to return to the union. The war led to no territorial changes, but Sweden was forced to pay a [war indemnity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reparations "War reparations") of 1 million silver [riksdaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riksdaler "Riksdaler") to Denmark, an amount known as the _[Älvsborg ransom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Stettin\_(1570) "Treaty of Stettin (1570)")_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-48) King Christian used this money to found several towns and fortresses, most notably [Glückstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gl%C3%BCckstadt "Glückstadt") (founded as a rival to [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg")) and [Christiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo"). Inspired by the [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company"), he founded a similar [Danish company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_East_India_Company "Danish East India Company") and planned to claim Ceylon as a colony, but the company only managed to acquire [Tranquebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tharangambadi "Tharangambadi") on India's [Coromandel Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coromandel_Coast "Coromandel Coast").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-49)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-50) Denmark's large colonial aspirations included a few key [trading posts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_posts "Trading posts") in Africa and India. While Denmark's trading posts in India were of little note, it played an important role in the highly lucrative [Atlantic slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade "Atlantic slave trade"), through its trading outposts in [Fort Christiansborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osu_Castle "Osu Castle") in [Osu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osu,_Accra "Osu, Accra"), [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana") through which 1.5 million slaves were traded.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-guardian6nov2018-51)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-52) While the Danish colonial empire was sustained by trade with other major powers, and [plantations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation "Plantation") – ultimately a lack of resources led to its stagnation.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-53)

In the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War"), Christian tried to become the leader of the [Lutheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") states in Germany but suffered a crushing defeat at the [Battle of Lutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lutter "Battle of Lutter").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker198478-54) The result was that the Catholic army under [Albrecht von Wallenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albrecht_von_Wallenstein "Albrecht von Wallenstein") was able to invade, occupy, and pillage Jutland, forcing Denmark [to withdraw from the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_L%C3%BCbeck "Treaty of Lübeck").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker198479-55) Denmark managed to avoid territorial concessions, but King [Gustavus Adolphus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavus_Adolphus_of_Sweden "Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden")' intervention in Germany was seen as a sign that the military power of Sweden was on the rise while Denmark's influence in the region was declining. Swedish armies [invaded Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torstenson_War "Torstenson War") in 1643 and claimed Scania in 1644. In the 1645 [Treaty of Brømsebro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Treaty_of_Br%C3%B6msebro_(1645) "Second Treaty of Brömsebro (1645)"), Denmark surrendered Halland, [Gotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotland "Gotland"), the last parts of Danish Estonia, and several provinces in Norway.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Stormen_p%C3%A5_K%C3%B8benhavn_%28F.C._Lund%29.jpg/330px-Stormen_p%C3%A5_K%C3%B8benhavn_%28F.C._Lund%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stormen_p%C3%A5_K%C3%B8benhavn_(F.C._Lund).jpg)

The [Assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_on_Copenhagen_(1659) "Assault on Copenhagen (1659)") on [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen") on 11 February 1659 during the [Second Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Northern_War "Second Northern War"). Danish defenders under King [Frederick III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_III_of_Denmark "Frederick III of Denmark") successfully repelled the forces of the [Swedish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Empire "Swedish Empire"). Painting by [Frederik Christian Lund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederik_Christian_Lund "Frederik Christian Lund").

Seeing an opportunity to tear up the Treaty of Brømsebro, King [Frederick III of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_III_of_Denmark "Frederick III of Denmark"), in 1657, declared war on Sweden, the latter being deeply involved in the [Second Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Northern_War "Second Northern War") (1655–1660), and marched on [Bremen-Verden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen-Verden "Bremen-Verden"). This led to a massive Danish defeat as the armies of King [Charles X Gustav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_X_Gustav "Charles X Gustav") of Sweden conquered [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland") and, following the [Swedish March across](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_Across_the_Belts "March Across the Belts") the frozen [Danish Straits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Straits "Danish Straits"), occupied [Funen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funen "Funen") and much of [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand "Zealand") before signing the [Peace of Roskilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Roskilde "Treaty of Roskilde") in February 1658, which gave Sweden control of Scania, [Blekinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blekinge "Blekinge"), [Bohuslän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohusl%C3%A4n "Bohuslän"), [Trøndelag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndelag "Trøndelag"), and the island of [Bornholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bornholm "Bornholm"). Charles X Gustav quickly regretted not having ruined Denmark and in August 1658, he launched a [second attack on Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dano-Swedish_War_(1658%E2%80%931660) "Dano-Swedish War (1658–1660)"), conquered most of the Danish islands, and began a two-year-long siege of [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"). King Frederick III actively led the defence of the city, rallying its citizens to take up arms, and [repelled the Swedish attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_on_Copenhagen_(1659) "Assault on Copenhagen (1659)").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIsacson2002229-56)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglund2000610-57) The siege ended following the death of Charles X Gustav in 1660.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStoneBainBoothParnell200835-58) In the ensuing [peace settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Copenhagen_(1660) "Treaty of Copenhagen (1660)"), Denmark managed to maintain its independence and regain control of Trøndelag and Bornholm.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrost2000180%E2%80%93183-59) Attaining great popularity following the war, Frederick III used this to [disband the elective monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Law "King's Law") in favour of [absolute monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy "Absolute monarchy"), which lasted until 1848 in Denmark.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-60)

Denmark tried but failed to regain control of Scania in the [Scanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanian_War "Scanian War") (1675–1679). After the [Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War "Great Northern War") (1700–21), Denmark managed to regain control of the parts of [Schleswig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig "Schleswig") and [Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holstein "Holstein") ruled by the house of [Holstein-Gottorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holstein-Gottorp "Holstein-Gottorp") in the 1720 [Treaty of Frederiksborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frederiksborg "Treaty of Frederiksborg") and the 1773 [Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tsarskoye_Selo "Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo"), respectively. Denmark prospered greatly in the last decades of the 18th century due to its [neutral status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_neutrality_(international_relations) "Country neutrality (international relations)") allowing it to trade with both sides in the many contemporary wars. In the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars"), Denmark traded with both [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire "First French Empire") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") and joined the [League of Armed Neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_League_of_Armed_Neutrality "Second League of Armed Neutrality") with [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire"), Sweden, and [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Prussia "Kingdom of Prussia").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-61) British fears that Denmark-Norway would ally with France led to two attacks against Danish targets in Copenhagen in [1801](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Copenhagen_(1801) "Battle of Copenhagen (1801)") and [1807](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Copenhagen_(1807) "Battle of Copenhagen (1807)"). These attacks resulted in the British capturing most of the Dano-Norwegian navy and led to the outbreak of the [Gunboat War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunboat_War "Gunboat War"). In 1807 much of Copenhagen was burned down as a result of these bombardments, including Vor Frue Kirke, the main Danish cathedral. British control of the waterways between Denmark and Norway proved disastrous to the union's economy and in 1813 Denmark–Norway went bankrupt.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The union was dissolved by the [Treaty of Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Kiel "Treaty of Kiel") in 1814; the Danish monarchy "irrevocably and forever" renounced claims to the Kingdom of Norway in favour of the Swedish king.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-62) Denmark kept the possessions of Iceland (which retained the Danish monarchy until 1944), the [Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands") and [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), all of which had been governed by Norway for centuries.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-63) Apart from the Nordic colonies, Denmark continued to rule over [Danish India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_India "Danish India") from 1620 to 1869, the [Danish Gold Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Gold_Coast "Danish Gold Coast") (Ghana) from 1658 to 1850, and the [Danish West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_West_Indies "Danish West Indies") from 1671 to 1917.

### Constitutional monarchy (1849–present)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Grundlovgivende_rigsforsamling_-_Constantin_Hansen_full.jpg/250px-Grundlovgivende_rigsforsamling_-_Constantin_Hansen_full.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grundlovgivende_rigsforsamling_-_Constantin_Hansen_full.jpg)

The National Constitutional Assembly was convened by King [Frederick VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_VII_of_Denmark "Frederick VII of Denmark") in 1848 to adopt the [Constitution of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Denmark "Constitution of Denmark").

A nascent Danish liberal and national movement gained momentum in the 1830s; after the European [Revolutions of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848 "Revolutions of 1848"), Denmark peacefully became a [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy") on 5 June 1849. A new constitution established a [two-chamber parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigsdagen "Rigsdagen"). Denmark faced war against both [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia") and the [Austrian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Empire "Austrian Empire") in what became known as the [Second Schleswig War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Schleswig_War "Second Schleswig War"), lasting from February to October 1864. Denmark was defeated and obliged to [cede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cession "Cession")[Schleswig and Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Schleswig-Holstein "Province of Schleswig-Holstein") to Prussia. This loss came as the latest in the long series of defeats and [territorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Royal_Enclaves "Danish Royal Enclaves") losses that had begun in the 17th century. After these events, Denmark pursued a policy of neutrality in Europe.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-64)

[Industrialisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialisation "Industrialisation") came to Denmark in the second half of the 19th century.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-65) The [nation's first railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rail_transport_in_Denmark "History of rail transport in Denmark") were constructed in the 1850s, and improved communications and overseas trade allowed industry to develop in spite of Denmark's lack of natural resources. [Trade unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_union "Trade union") developed, starting in the 1870s. There was a considerable migration of people from the countryside to the cities, and Danish agriculture became centred on the export of dairy and meat products.

Denmark [maintained its neutral stance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_during_World_War_I "Denmark during World War I") during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). After the defeat of Germany, the [Versailles powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles "Treaty of Versailles") offered to return the region of Schleswig-Holstein to Denmark. Fearing German [irredentism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irredentism "Irredentism"), Denmark refused to consider the return of the area without a [plebiscite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebiscite "Plebiscite"); the two [Schleswig Plebiscites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig_Plebiscites "Schleswig Plebiscites") took place on 10 February and 14 March 1920, respectively. On 10 July 1920, Northern Schleswig was recovered by Denmark, thereby adding some 163,600 inhabitants and 3,984 square kilometres (1,538 sq mi). The country's first social democratic government took office in 1924.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Politico-66)

In 1939, Denmark signed a 10-year nonaggression pact with [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"). However, [Germany invaded Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_Denmark_(1940) "German invasion of Denmark (1940)") on 9 April 1940, and the Danish government quickly surrendered. Because roughly 10% of the German army's food supply depended on Danish agriculture, the occupation remained relatively cooperative compared to other European nations to ensure continued output. [World War II in Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_in_World_War_II "Denmark in World War II") was characterised by economic co-operation with Germany until 1943, when the Danish government refused further co-operation and [its navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Danish_Navy "Royal Danish Navy")[scuttled most of its ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Safari "Operation Safari") and sent many of its officers to Sweden, which was neutral. At that point the government fell. The [Danish resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_resistance_movement "Danish resistance movement") performed a [rescue operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_of_the_Danish_Jews "Rescue of the Danish Jews") that managed to evacuate several thousand [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Denmark "History of the Jews in Denmark") and their families to safety in Sweden before the Germans could send them to death camps. Some Danes supported [Nazism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazism "Nazism") by joining the [Danish Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Workers'_Party_of_Denmark "National Socialist Workers' Party of Denmark") or volunteering to fight with Germany as part of the [Frikorps Danmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frikorps_Danmark "Frikorps Danmark").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-67) Iceland severed ties with Denmark and [became an independent republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_the_republic_of_Iceland "Founding of the republic of Iceland") in 1944; [Germany surrendered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_of_Denmark "Liberation of Denmark") in May 1945. In 1948, the Faroe Islands gained [home rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_rule "Home rule"). In 1949, Denmark became a founding member of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO").

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_%28081%29.jpg/250px-Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_%28081%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tratado_de_Lisboa_13_12_2007_(081).jpg)

Denmark became a member of the European Union in 1973 and signed the [Lisbon Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Treaty "Lisbon Treaty") in 2007.

Denmark was a founding member of the [European Free Trade Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") (EFTA). During the 1960s, the EFTA countries were often referred to as the [Outer Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Seven "Outer Seven"), as opposed to the [Inner Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Six "Inner Six") of what was then the [European Economic Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Community "European Economic Community") (EEC).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-68) In 1973, along with Britain and Ireland, Denmark joined the European Economic Community (now the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union")) after a [public referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Danish_European_Communities_membership_referendum "1972 Danish European Communities membership referendum"). The [Maastricht Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty "Maastricht Treaty"), which involved further European integration, [was rejected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Danish_Maastricht_Treaty_referendum "1992 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum") by the Danish people in 1992; it was only accepted after a [second referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Danish_Maastricht_Treaty_referendum "1993 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum") in 1993, which provided for [four opt-outs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union "Opt-outs in the European Union") from policies. The Danes rejected the euro as the national currency in [a referendum in 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Danish_euro_referendum "2000 Danish euro referendum"). Constitutional change in 1953 led to a [single-chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameralism "Unicameralism") parliament elected by proportional representation, female accession to the Danish throne, and Greenland becoming an integral part of Denmark. Since 2025 the Danish territory of [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland") has been the target of [US hybrid warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_crisis "Greenland crisis") under [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-dab-72)[Mette Frederiksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mette_Frederiksen "Mette Frederiksen") said that "the Kingdom of Denmark—and thus Greenland—is a member of NATO and is therefore covered by the Alliance's [collective security guarantee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_5 "North Atlantic Treaty") [...] I [...] strongly urge the United States to cease its threats against a historically close ally."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-mefr-73)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Denmark "Geography of Denmark")

See also: [Geography of the Faroe Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_the_Faroe_Islands "Geography of the Faroe Islands") and [Geography of Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Greenland "Geography of Greenland")

[![Image 24: Satellite image](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Satellite_image_of_Denmark_in_July_2001.jpg/250px-Satellite_image_of_Denmark_in_July_2001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Satellite_image_of_Denmark_in_July_2001.jpg)

A satellite image of Jutland and the Danish islands

Located in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe"), on a latitude traversing southern [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), and being north of [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), Denmark[[N 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-proper-20) consists of the northern part of the [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland") peninsula and an [archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archipelago "Archipelago") of [406 islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Denmark "List of islands of Denmark").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-islands-22) Of these, the largest island is [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand "Zealand"), on which the capital [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen") is situated, on the same latitude as Moscow, and [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), followed by the [North Jutlandic Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Jutlandic_Island "North Jutlandic Island"), [Funen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funen "Funen"), and [Lolland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lolland "Lolland").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-75) The island of [Bornholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bornholm "Bornholm"), and small [archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archipelago "Archipelago") of [Ertholmene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ertholmene "Ertholmene") (_Christiansø_ colloqually, after its biggest islet), is located some 150 km east of the rest of the country, in the [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea "Baltic Sea"). Many of the larger islands are connected by bridges; a [bridge-tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund_Bridge "Øresund Bridge") across the [Øresund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund "Øresund") connects Zealand with Sweden; the [Great Belt Fixed Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Belt_Fixed_Link "Great Belt Fixed Link") connects Funen with Zealand; and the [Little Belt Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Belt_Bridge_(1970) "Little Belt Bridge (1970)") connects Jutland with Funen. [Ferries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferry "Ferry") or [small aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_aircraft "Small aircraft") connect to the smaller islands. The four [cities with populations over 100,000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Denmark_by_population "List of cities in Denmark by population") are the capital Copenhagen on Zealand; [Aarhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus "Aarhus") and [Aalborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aalborg "Aalborg") in Jutland; and [Odense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odense "Odense") on Funen.

[![Image 25: A labelled map of Denmark](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Da-map.png/250px-Da-map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Da-map.png)

The metropolitan part occupies a total area of 42,943.9 [square kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_kilometre "Square kilometre") (16,581 sq mi).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-area-76) The area of inland water is 600 km 2 (232 sq mi).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJensen199910-77) The size of the land area cannot be stated exactly since the ocean constantly erodes and adds material to the coastline, and because of human [land reclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation "Land reclamation") projects (to counter erosion). [Post-glacial rebound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-glacial_rebound "Post-glacial rebound") raises the land by a bit less than 1 cm (0.4 in) a year in the north and east, extending the coast. A circle enclosing the same area as Denmark would be 234 kilometres (145 miles) in [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter "Diameter") with a [circumference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumference "Circumference") of 736 km (457 mi) (land area only: 232.33 km (144.36 mi) and 730 km (454 mi) respectively). The land area is the size of the [Upper Peninsula of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Peninsula_of_Michigan "Upper Peninsula of Michigan"). It shares a border of 68 kilometres (42 mi) with Germany to the south and is otherwise surrounded by 8,750 km (5,437 mi) of tidal [shoreline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoreline "Shoreline") (including small [bays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay "Bay") and [inlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inlet "Inlet")).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-Nature_and_Environment-78) No location in Denmark is farther from the coast than 52 km (32 mi). On the south-west coast of Jutland, the tide is between 1 and 2 m (3.28 and 6.56 ft), and the tideline moves outward and inward on a 10 km (6.2 mi) stretch.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-79) Denmark's [territorial waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_of_Denmark "Borders of Denmark") total 105,000 square kilometres (40,541 square miles).

Denmark's northernmost point is [Skagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skagen "Skagen") point (the north beach of the Skaw) at 57° 45' 7" northern latitude; the southernmost is [Gedser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gedser "Gedser") point (the southern tip of [Falster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falster "Falster")) at 54° 33' 35" northern latitude; the westernmost point is [Blåvandshuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bl%C3%A5vandshuk "Blåvandshuk") at 8° 4' 22" eastern longitude; and the easternmost point is [Østerskær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98stersk%C3%A6r "Østerskær") at 15° 11' 55" eastern longitude. This is in the small [Ertholmene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ertholmene "Ertholmene") archipelago 18 kilometres (11 mi) north-east of Bornholm. The distance from east to west is 452 kilometres (281 mi), from north to south 368 kilometres (229 mi).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-80)

The highest natural point is [Møllehøj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B8lleh%C3%B8j "Møllehøj"), at 170.86 metres (560.56 ft).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-81) Although this is by far the lowest high point in the Nordic countries and also less than half of the highest point in [Southern Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6taland "Götaland"), Denmark's general elevation in its interior is generally at a safe level from [rising sea levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level_rise "Sea level rise"). [Lammefjorden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lammefjorden "Lammefjorden"), deeper than −7 m (−23 ft) (near Audebo), is the lowest point. Lake [Arresø](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arres%C3%B8 "Arresø"), located northwest of Copenhagen, is the largest lake.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJensen199910-77)

| Country (west of Norway) | National instrument (as of May 2024) | Source |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------|---------|
| Sweden | **Nyckelharpa** – a keyed bowed lyre that is considered Sweden’s quintessential national instrument | 【28†L10-L15】 |

*Explanation*

- **Northernmost country using such an instrument as its national symbol** – *Norway*, whose national instrument is the **Hardanger fiddle** (a bowed fiddle with metal strings). 【26†L137-L140】  
- **Directly west of Norway** – the only land‑adjacent country is **Sweden**.  
  - Sweden’s national instrument is the **nyckelharpa**, a keyed bowed lyre that fits the description of “metal, gut or horsehair strings and open strings” and is an established variant used by several Nordic countries.【28†L10-L15】

Thus, as of May 2024, the national instrument of the country directly west of the northernmost such country (Norway) is Sweden’s *nyckelharpa*. No other country lies directly west of Norway that is recognised as having a national instrument of this type.

**Countries directly west of the northernmost country that uses a variant of this open‑string, metal/gut/horsehair fiddle as its national instrument**

| Country (west of Norway) | National instrument (as of May 2024) | Source |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------|---------|
| Sweden | **Nyckelharpa** – a keyed bowed lyre that is considered Sweden’s quintessential national instrument | 【28†L10-L15】 |

*Explanation*

- **Northernmost country using such an instrument as its national symbol** – *Norway*, whose national instrument is the **Hardanger fiddle** (a bowed fiddle with metal strings). 【26†L137-L140】  
- **Directly west of Norway** – the only land‑adjacent country is **Sweden**.  
  - Sweden’s national instrument is the **nyckelharpa**, a keyed bowed lyre that fits the description of “metal, gut or horsehair strings and open strings” and is an established variant used by several Nordic countries.【28†L10-L15】

Thus, as of May 2024, the national instrument of the country directly west of the northernmost such country (Norway) is Sweden’s *nyckelharpa*. No other country lies directly west of Norway that is recognised as having a national instrument of this type.
